title: About
text: This is the Python documentation of circlize-py — a pure-Python port of Zuguang Gu’s circlize package for circular visualization, built on numpy, pandas, matplotlib, scipy, and Pillow. Examples in this book are generated under circlize_py version 0.4.16 (matching R circlize v0.4.16). If you use circlize / circlize-py in your publications, please cite the original paper: Gu, Z. (2014) circlize implements and enhances circular visualization in R. Bioinformatics, 30(19), 2811–2812. DOI: 10.1093/bioinformatics/btu393 Circular Visualization in Python cover

title: Installation
text: From the repository root (requires Python >= 3.10): pip install -e ".[dev]" Once installed, both top-level package names can be imported interchangeably: import circlize_py # or import circlize

title: Indexing & key conventions
text: To combine Python conventions cleanly with faithful R circlize porting, keep the following indexing rules in mind: 1-based track_index and CELL_META.sector.numeric.index vs. 0-based heatmap rows: track_index is 1-based (1, 2, ..., n_tracks), matching R circlize (track_index=1 is the outermost track). CELL_META.sector.numeric.index (or CELL_META.sector_numeric_index) is 1-based (1..n_sectors), matching R; CELL_META.sector_idx gives the 0-based Python sector position (0..n_sectors - 1). Heatmap row selectors follow 0-based Python indexing: CELL_META.subset and CELL_META.row_order contain 0-based row indices (0..n_rows - 1), and circos.heatmap.link(row_ind1, row_ind2) and circos.heatmap.get.x(row_ind) accept either 0-based integer indices or row-name strings. Genomic value column selectors: Column-name strings (e.g., numeric_column="value1", labels_column="gene") and 0-based integer indices are supported, with automatic 1-based fallback when idx == df.shape[1] for compatibility with R BED scripts. Literal padding with I(...): Import from circlize_py import I when passing raw data-coordinate values to padding=I([...]) in highlight.sector(...). Colors and coordinate matrices: All 657 R named colors (e.g., "grey50", "red3"), R palette indices 1..8, #RRGGBB / #RRGGBBAA hex strings, and Matplotlib colors work natively. circlize() and reverse.circlize() return a NamedMatrix2D supporting NumPy indexing (pos[0, 0]), named column selection (pos[:, "theta"]), and attribute access (pos.theta, pos.rou, pos.x, pos.y).

title: 1 Introduction
text: Circular layouts are effective for representing complex, multi-layered information. First, they compactly display data with long axes or many categories; second, they intuitively align multiple measurements on the same object across stacked tracks; third, they clearly reveal relationships between elements via interior links or ribbons. Circos pioneered circular layout visualization in Perl, becoming especially influential in genomics—so much so that circular plots are commonly called “circos plots”. circlize brought that expressive circular grammar into R, and circlize-py brings the full design directly into Python on top of numpy, pandas, matplotlib, scipy, and Pillow. Rather than wrapping an external binary or generating static configuration files, circlize-py integrates natively with Python data structures and Matplotlib figures while keeping the flexibility and configurability of Circos. In this book, Part I introduces the general circular layout and graphics engine. Part II covers functions specifically designed for genomic datasets. Part III presents a comprehensive guide to visualizing relationships with Chord diagrams, and Part IV explores creative uses of the library.

title: 1.1 Principle of design
text: A circular layout is composed of sectors and tracks. Different categories are allocated into distinct sectors around the circle, while multiple measurements on the same category are arranged as concentric tracks stacked from the outside of the circle toward the center. The intersection of a sector and a track is called a cell (or grid, panel), which is the basic plotting unit in a circular layout—an imaginary rectangular plotting region mapped onto polar coordinates. Because complex charts are built out of simple geometric primitives such as points, lines, and polygons, circlize-py implements low-level graphic functions inside circular cells so arbitrary high-level visualizations can be composed without artificial restrictions. Currently, circlize-py provides the following low-level graphic functions (mirroring R’s base graphics names with a circos. prefix or circos_ snake_case alias): circos.points() (circos_points()): adds points in a cell. circos.lines() (circos_lines()): adds lines or filled area curves in a cell. circos.segments() (circos_segments()): adds line segments in a cell. circos.rect() (circos_rect()): adds curved rectangles in a cell. circos.polygon() (circos_polygon()): adds polygons in a cell. circos.text() (circos_text()): adds rotated or curved text in a cell. circos.axis() and circos.yaxis(): add circular x-axes and radial y-axes in a cell. The following function draws connections between two positions across the circle: circos.link() (circos_link()) The following functions draw high-level graphics: circos.barplot(): draws simple or stacked circular barplots. circos.boxplot(): draws circular boxplots. circos.violin(): draws circular violin plots. circos.heatmap(): draws split circular heatmaps with clustering. circos.raster(): draws raster images inside cells. circos.arrow(): draws circular arrows. The following functions arrange and manage the circular layout: circos.initialize(): allocates sectors on the circle. circos.track() (or circos.trackPlotRegion()): creates plotting regions for all cells in a track. circos.update() (or circos.updatePlotRegion()): clears and updates an existing cell. circos.par(): reads or sets global layout parameters. circos.info(): prints or plots metadata of the current circular plot. circos.clear(): resets graphic parameters and internal layout state. Together, these building blocks allow you to create almost any kind of circular figure. The showcase composite below displays nine diverse circular visualizations generated directly with circlize-py. title: 1.2 A quick glance
text: Before diving into full details, let’s walk through a complete multi-track example step by step to see how circlize-py works in practice. First, generate a synthetic dataset with a categorical sectors column, numeric x values, and numeric y values: import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd from circlize_py import CELL_META, circos, mm_y, rand_color rng = np.random.default_rng(999) n = 1000 df = pd.DataFrame( { "sectors": rng.choice(list("abcdefgh"), size=n, replace=True), "x": rng.normal(size=n), "y": rng.uniform(size=n), } ) Next, initialize the circular layout. The circle is partitioned into sectors according to the x-range within each category. When x is supplied to circos.initialize(), x is grouped by sectors and each sector’s angular width is set proportionally to its data span. By default, sectors start at $= 0^$ (3 o’clock in standard polar coordinates) and proceed clockwise around the circle. Calling circos.initialize() records the geometry internally without drawing visible marks until the first track is added: fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.2, 6.2), dpi=140) circos.par(track_height=0.1, points_overflow_warning=False) circos.initialize(df["sectors"], x=df["x"]) Here, circos.par(track_height=0.1) sets the default radial height of newly created tracks to 0.1. Because circlize-py always draws inside the unit circle (radius 1), 0.1 corresponds to 10% of the circle radius. (See Section 2.7.2 for specifying heights in physical units such as mm or cm.) Notice that sector allocation only needs x-direction values (along the circumference); y-direction values (along the radius) are specified when creating individual tracks. Once initialized, graphics are built track by track from the outside inward. Always create a track with circos.track() (or circos.trackPlotRegion()) before calling low-level plotting functions inside its cells—analogous to creating a Matplotlib Axes before calling plot() or scatter(). Because x-ranges are fixed at initialization, circos.track() only requires y (to derive y-ranges automatically) or an explicit ylim=(ymin, ymax) pair shared across the track: def panel_t1(x, y): circos.text( CELL_META.xcenter, CELL_META.cell.ylim[1] + mm_y(5), CELL_META.sector_index, ) circos.axis(labels_cex=0.6) circos.track(df["sectors"], y=df["y"], panel_fun=panel_t1) col = ["#FF0000", "#00FF00"] * 4 circos.trackPoints(df["sectors"], df["x"], df["y"], col=col, pch=16, cex=0.5) circos.text(-1, 0.5, "text", sector_index="a", track_index=1) First example of circlize-py: add the first track. Axes are usually placed along the outer rim of the outermost track. Inside panel_fun, circos.track() visits each cell in order and sets that cell as the “current” cell immediately after creating its plotting region (detailed further in Section 2.6). Calling circos.axis() inside panel_fun draws an x-axis along the top (outside) edge of every cell. Sector names are placed outside the first track using circos.text() and CELL_META metadata. Adding mm_y(5) shifts the text 5 mm radially outward in the cell’s data coordinates (see Section 2.7.2). Setting points_overflow_warning=False in circos.par() suppresses warnings when drawing labels outside cell borders. Alternatively, sector labels can be placed in a dedicated borderless outer track (as circos.initializeWithIdeogram() in Chapter 9 and chordDiagram() in Chapter 14 do). After creating the track, circos.trackPoints() adds scatter points across all cells simultaneously. As discussed in Section 3.2, placing circos.points() inside panel_fun is generally more flexible, though circos.trackPoints() is convenient for simple scatter tracks. Low-level functions like circos.text() can also be called outside panel_fun by supplying sector_index and track_index explicitly (track_index defaults to the most recently created track). Now add histograms on the second track using circos.trackHist(), a high-level track function that creates a new track automatically. Fixing bin_size=0.2 e

title: 2.1 Coordinate transformation
text: Mapping data onto a circle involves transformations across three coordinate systems. First is the data coordinate system, where x and y ranges match the scale of your input data in each cell. Second is the polar coordinate system, which maps each rectangular cell onto a circular arc (theta, rou). Third is the canvas coordinate system, where graphics are rendered onto the Matplotlib Axes (Figure 2.1). Each cell maintains its own independent data coordinate frame. circlize-py transforms (x, y) from data coordinates to polar coordinates and then to Cartesian canvas coordinates automatically, so you can think of every cell as a familiar rectangular plotting box. Transformation between different coordinates The canvas coordinate system corresponds to standard Matplotlib data coordinates spanning (-1, 1) on both the x- and y-axes by default with an equal (1:1) aspect ratio. The circular plot is always drawn inside the unit circle (radius 1) and built sequentially from the outside inward.

title:
2.2 Rules for making the
circular plot
text: Constructing a circular figure follows a simple, strict lifecycle: initialize layout -> create track -> add graphics -> create track -> add graphics -> ... -> clear. Graphics can be added to any cell once its track exists. Order of drawing circular layout Initialize the layout with circos.initialize(). Because circular layouts organize data across categories, at least one categorical variable (sectors) is required. Sector x-ranges can be supplied via x or xlim (see Section 2.3). Create a track and add graphics. Each new track is placed immediately inside the previous one. Low-level graphics can only be drawn after the track is created. There are three ways to populate cells in a track: Create the track first, then call low-level functions such as circos.points() and circos.lines() sector-by-sector inside a for loop with explicit sector_index. Use batch functions such as circos.trackPoints() or circos.trackLines() to split vectors by sectors and draw across all cells at once. Pass a panel_fun(x, y) callback to circos.track(), which runs immediately as each cell is created and automatically receives that cell’s subset of x and y. This is the recommended pattern (see Section 2.6). Repeat step 2 for additional inner tracks until you reach the desired inner radius. Call circos.clear() to reset layout state and global parameters before making another plot. The three plotting patterns look like this in Python: Pattern 1 — Explicit for loop after track creation: circos.initialize(sectors, xlim=xlim) circos.track(ylim=ylim) for sector_index in all_sector_index: circos.points(x1, y1, sector_index=sector_index) circos.lines(x2, y2, sector_index=sector_index) Notice that track_index can be omitted immediately after circos.track(), because the newly created track is automatically marked as the “current” track. Pattern 2 — Batch track functions: circos.initialize(sectors, xlim=xlim) circos.track(ylim=ylim) circos.trackPoints(sectors, x, y) circos.trackLines(sectors, x, y) circos.trackPoints() and circos.trackLines() internally loop over sectors and call circos.points() / circos.lines(). They are convenient for quick single-layer tracks, though panel_fun offers much greater flexibility. Pattern 3 — panel_fun callback (recommended): circos.initialize(sectors, xlim=xlim) def panel_fn(x, y): circos.points(x, y) circos.lines(x, y) circos.track(sectors, x=all_x, y=all_y, ylim=ylim, panel_fun=panel_fn) Because circlize-py updates the internal current sector and track index before invoking panel_fun on each cell, low-level functions inside panel_fun automatically target the active cell without needing sector_index or track_index.

title: 2.3 Sectors and tracks
text: A circular layout is a 2D grid of sectors (angular wedges) and tracks (concentric rings). In the diagram below, the red ring highlights one track and the blue wedge highlights one sector; their intersection is a single cell. Sectors and tracks in circular layout Sectors are allocated by circos.initialize(). Each unique category becomes one sector whose angular width is proportional to its x-range. You can supply a numeric array x matching the length of sectors (so min/max x-ranges are computed per sector), or supply xlim directly as either a (n_sectors, 2) NumPy array / DataFrame or a length-2 [xmin, xmax] sequence shared across all sectors. If a DataFrame with a named index is passed as xlim, sectors can be omitted and row index labels become the sector names: circos.initialize(sectors, x=x) circos.initialize(sectors, xlim=xlim) circos.initialize(xlim=xlim_df) After circos.initialize(), the layout geometry is recorded internally, though nothing is visible on the Matplotlib canvas until at least one track is drawn. Sector order on the circle is determined by sectors: If sectors is a pandas.Categorical (or categorical Series), sectors follow the explicit category order (categories). Just like R’s factor(sectors), pd.Categorical(sectors) sorts category names alphabetically by default, whereas pd.Categorical(sectors, categories=sectors, ordered=True) preserves the exact order given in sectors. If sectors is a plain Python list or array with unique values (no duplicates), circos.initialize() preserves its insertion order; if sectors contains repeated entries (e.g., data rows belonging to 8 categories), unique categories are sorted alphabetically unless wrapped in pd.Categorical(..., categories=...). import pandas as pd sectors = ["d", "f", "e", "c", "g", "b", "a"] s1 = pd.Categorical(sectors) circos.initialize(s1, xlim=[0, 1]) s2 = pd.Categorical(sectors, categories=sectors, ordered=True) circos.initialize(s2, xlim=[0, 1]) Different sector orders Cells in the same sector share the same x-range across all tracks. Consequently, each call to circos.track() only needs a y-range (y or ylim), typically shared across all cells in that track. Passing x to circos.track() is optional and simply forwards per-sector x subsets into panel_fun(x, y): circos.track(sectors, y=y) circos.track(sectors, ylim=[0, 1]) circos.track(sectors, x=x, y=y, panel_fun=...) If sectors is omitted in circos.track(), cells are created for all initialized sectors. If sectors covers only a subset of sectors, cells in the remaining sectors are still created internally without visible borders so track geometry stays aligned: # Only sectors present in `sectors_subset` draw visible borders circos.track(sectors_subset, y=y) # All initialized sectors draw visible borders circos.track(ylim=[0, 1]) circos.track(ylim=[float(y.min()), float(y.max())]) Once created, each cell acts as an independent rectangular region with its own xlim and ylim, and sector and x-axis directions can be configured independently via circos.par().
