title: 2.4 Graphic parameters
text: Global layout options are managed through circos.par(). Several options affect sector allocation and therefore must be set before circos.initialize(): start_degree (start.degree): Polar angle (in degrees, counter-clockwise from 3 o’clock) where the first sector begins. Setting start_degree=90 starts at 12 o’clock. gap_degree / gap_after (gap.degree / gap.after): Angular gap in degrees between adjacent sectors. Accepts a scalar, a list matching the number of sectors, or a dict keyed by sector names. The first gap is placed after the first sector. Modifying either gap_degree or gap_after updates both. track_margin (track.margin): Two-element sequence [bottom_margin, top_margin] outside cell borders as fractions of the unit circle radius (or converted via mm_h() / cm_h() / inch_h()). cell_padding (cell.padding): Four-element sequence [bottom, left, top, right] inside cell borders. Indices 0 and 2 (bottom/top) are fractions of the unit circle radius (or mm_h()/cm_h()), while indices 1 and 3 (left/right) are measured in degrees. unit_circle_segments (unit.circle.segments): Number of straight line segments approximating a full unit circle (2 * pi / unit_circle_segments controls curve smoothness). track_height (track.height): Default radial height of tracks as a fraction of the unit circle radius (includes bottom/top cell_padding, excludes track_margin). Can be set using mm_h(), cm_h(), or inch_h(). points_overflow_warning (points.overflow.warning): Whether to emit a UserWarning when graphics extend outside a cell’s plotting region. Set to False when placing sector labels outside Track 1. canvas_xlim, canvas_ylim (canvas.xlim, canvas.ylim): Canvas limits on the Matplotlib Axes (default [-1.0, 1.0]). Setting canvas_xlim=[0, 1], canvas_ylim=[0, 1], for instance, displays only the upper-right quadrant. circle_margin (circle.margin): Positive margins outside the unit circle of length 1 (all sides), 2 ([lr, bt]), or 4 ([left, right, bottom, top]), expanding canvas_xlim and canvas_ylim automatically. clock_wise (clock.wise): Whether sectors proceed clockwise (True, default) or counter-clockwise (False). xaxis_clock_wise (xaxis.clock.wise): Direction of the x-axis inside every cell (True = clockwise, default; False = counter-clockwise). Regions in a cell Default values of circos.par() are summarized below: Parameter Default value start_degree (start.degree) 0.0 gap_degree / gap_after 1.0 track_margin (track.margin) [0.01, 0.01] cell_padding (cell.padding) [0.02, 1.0, 0.02, 1.0] unit_circle_segments 500 track_height (track.height) 0.2 points_overflow_warning True canvas_xlim (canvas.xlim) [-1.0, 1.0] canvas_ylim (canvas.ylim) [-1.0, 1.0] circle_margin (circle.margin) [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] clock_wise (clock.wise) True xaxis_clock_wise (xaxis.clock.wise) True Parameters controlling sector allocation (start_degree, gap_degree/gap_after, canvas_xlim, canvas_ylim, circle_margin, clock_wise, and xaxis_clock_wise) must be configured before circos.initialize(), and left/right cell_padding (indices 1 and 3) cannot be changed afterward. Always call circos.clear() after finishing a plot so these options reset cleanly. circos.par() supports function calls, dictionary indexing, and attribute assignment interchangeably, and RESET=True restores defaults: from circlize_py import circos circos.par(start_degree=30) circos.par["start.degree"] = 30 circos.par.start_degree = 30 circos.par(RESET=True) print(circos.par) CircosPar(start.degree=0.0, gap.degree=1.0, track.margin=[0.01, 0.01], unit.circle.segments=500, cell.padding=[0.02, 1.0, 0.02, 1.0], track.height=0.2, points.overflow.warning=True, circle.margin=[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0], canvas.xlim=[-1.0, 1.0], canvas.ylim=[-1.0, 1.0], major.by.degree=10.0, clock.wise=True, xaxis.clock.wise=True, message=True) For layouts where sectors vary in order or subsetting (such as chordDiagram() in Chapter 14), gap_degree / gap_after can be passed as a dictionary keyed by sector names ({"a": 2, "b": 10, ...}), so gaps are auto

title: 2.5 Create plotting regions
text: A track’s plotting regions must be created with circos.track() (or circos.trackPlotRegion()) before drawing low-level primitives. At minimum, provide either y or ylim. When sectors, x, and y are supplied with matching lengths, circlize-py subsets them by sector and passes each cell’s slices to panel_fun. Styling arguments such as bg_border and bg_col accept either a scalar or a sequence matching the number of sectors (in sector order). Alternatively, you can customize individual cell backgrounds inside panel_fun using CELL_META.cell.xlim and CELL_META.cell.ylim: circos.rect( CELL_META.cell.xlim[0], CELL_META.cell.ylim[0], CELL_META.cell.xlim[1], CELL_META.cell.ylim[1], col="#FF000040", border=1, ) Passing track_margin or cell_padding directly to circos.track() overrides those settings for that track alone (left/right padding indices 1 and 3 remain fixed by initialization).

title: 2.6 Update plotting regions
text: Passing an existing track_index (1-based) to circos.track() re-creates the entire track—allowing ylim to change while keeping the track’s radial position and height fixed: circos.track(sectors, ylim=[0, 1], track_index=1, panel_fun=...) To erase and redraw a single cell while preserving its xlim and ylim, use circos.update() (or circos.updatePlotRegion()), which sets that cell as the active cell for subsequent low-level calls: circos.update(sector_index, track_index) circos.points(x, y)

title: 2.7 panel_fun argument
text: Passing panel_fun=... to circos.track() is the most idiomatic way to populate cells. Your callback accepts (x, y) containing the data points belonging to the current cell (or (None, None) if x/y were omitted in circos.track()): sectors = ["a", "a", "a", "b", "b"] x = np.arange(1, 6) y = np.arange(5, 0, -1) def panel_fn(x, y): circos.points(x, y) circos.track(sectors, x=x, y=y, panel_fun=panel_fn) You can also ignore (x, y) and subset arrays manually inside panel_fun using CELL_META.sector_index: sectors_arr = np.array(["a", "a", "a", "b", "b"]) x2 = np.arange(1, 6) y2 = np.arange(5, 0, -1) def panel_fn(x, y): mask = sectors_arr == CELL_META.sector_index circos.points(x2[mask], y2[mask]) circos.track(ylim=[1, 5], panel_fun=panel_fn) Because circos.track() sets the current sector and track before each panel_fun invocation, get_cell_meta_data(name) and its convenient proxy CELL_META both read metadata for the active cell automatically: sector.index (CELL_META.sector_index / CELL_META.sector.index): Sector name string. sector.numeric.index (CELL_META.sector_numeric_index): 1-based sector index (1..n_sectors), matching R; use CELL_META.sector_idx for 0-based 0..n_sectors - 1. track.index (CELL_META.track_index): 1-based track index (1..n_tracks). xlim, ylim: 2-element NumPy arrays [min, max] of the cell’s data coordinates. xcenter, ycenter: Midpoints of xlim and ylim. xrange, yrange: xlim[1] - xlim[0] and ylim[1] - ylim[0]. cell.xlim, cell.ylim: Data ranges extended by horizontal/vertical cell paddings. xplot: [start_degree, end_degree] of the cell in polar angles. yplot: [bottom_radius, top_radius] of the cell on the unit circle. cell.width, cell.height: Angular width (degrees) and radial height (unit-circle units). cell.start.degree, cell.end.degree, cell.bottom.radius, cell.top.radius: Scalar shortcuts for xplot and yplot. track.margin, cell.padding: Margin and padding lists for the cell. Using get_cell_meta_data() vs. CELL_META: from circlize_py import CELL_META, get_cell_meta_data # Explicit get_cell_meta_data() circos.track( ylim=ylim, panel_fun=lambda x, y: circos.text( get_cell_meta_data("xcenter"), get_cell_meta_data("ycenter"), get_cell_meta_data("sector.index"), ), ) # Concise CELL_META proxy (supports dot or bracket access) circos.track( ylim=ylim, panel_fun=lambda x, y: circos.text( CELL_META.xcenter, CELL_META.ycenter, CELL_META.sector_index, ), ) Because CELL_META always resolves the current cell, it is primarily used inside panel_fun. Outside panel_fun, call set_current_cell(sector_index, track_index) to target a specific cell across multiple statements: from circlize_py import set_current_cell set_current_cell(sector_index, track_index) circos.text(CELL_META.xcenter, CELL_META.ycenter, CELL_META.sector_index)

title:
2.8.1 circlize() and
reverse.circlize()
text: circlize() maps data coordinates (x, y) inside a cell to polar coordinates (theta, rou), while reverse.circlize() (or reverse_circlize()) maps polar (theta, rou) back to a cell’s data coordinates (x, y). Both return a NamedMatrix2D supporting NumPy slicing and named column access ([:, "theta"], .theta, .rou, .x, .y): from circlize_py import circos, circlize, reverse circos.initialize(["a", "b"], xlim=[0, 1]) circos.track(ylim=[0, 1]) print(circlize(0.5, 0.5, sector_index="a", track_index=1)) # NamedMatrix2D([[270.5 , 0.89]]) print(reverse.circlize(90, 0.9, sector_index="a", track_index=1)) # NamedMatrix2D([[1.51977401, 0.56 ]]) print(reverse.circlize(90, 0.9, sector_index="b", track_index=1)) # NamedMatrix2D([[0.50282486, 0.56 ]]) circos.clear() Notice that the same polar coordinate (90, 0.9) maps to two different data locations depending on which sector is queried. Chaining circlize -> reverse.circlize -> circlize lets multiple circular plots share and connect coordinates on the same page, which powers nested zooming in Chapter 13. To convert polar coordinates (theta, rou) to Cartesian canvas coordinates (x, y), circlize-py exports polar2Cartesian() (and polar_to_cartesian()). The example below renders all 32 bundled Keith Haring tiles from load_extdata("doodle") directly onto a Matplotlib Axes by transforming each cell center with polar2Cartesian(circlize(...)) (see Section 3.10 for the dedicated circos.raster() helper): import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from circlize_py import CELL_META, circos, circlize, load_extdata, mm_y, polar2Cartesian imgs = load_extdata("doodle") names = [f"tile_{i:02d}" for i in range(1, len(imgs) + 1)] fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.4, 6.4), dpi=140) circos.par(points_overflow_warning=False) circos.initialize(names, xlim=[0.0, 1.0]) ax = plt.gca() def panel_tile(x, y): pos = polar2Cartesian(circlize(CELL_META.xcenter, CELL_META.ycenter)) img = imgs[CELL_META.sector_numeric_index - 1] circos.text( CELL_META.xcenter, CELL_META.cell.ylim[0] - mm_y(2), CELL_META.sector_index, facing="clockwise", nice_facing=True, adj=[1.0, 0.5], cex=0.6, ) cx, cy = float(pos[0, 0]), float(pos[0, 1]) ax.imshow(img, extent=(cx - 0.04, cx + 0.04, cy - 0.04, cy + 0.04), origin="upper", zorder=3) circos.track(ylim=[0.0, 1.0], track_height=0.14, bg_border="black", panel_fun=panel_tile) ax.set_xlim(-1.05, 1.05) ax.set_ylim(-1.05, 1.05) circos.clear() Add raster images to the circular plot via polar2Cartesian

title: 2.8.2 Absolute units
text: Layout lengths such as track_height are specified in unit-circle radius units, whereas low-level plotting functions work in cell data coordinates. circlize-py provides conversion helpers so physical lengths (mm, cm, inches) map cleanly to either coordinate system: mm_h(x), cm_h(x), inch_h(x) / inches_h(x), and uh(x, unit) (convert_length() / convert_height()): convert physical units into canvas radius units (used for track_height, track_margin, and vertical cell_padding). Use strwidth_canvas() / strheight_canvas() to measure string dimensions in canvas units. mm_h(2) # 2 mm in canvas units cm_h(1) # 1 cm in canvas units mm_x(x), cm_x(x), inch_x(x) / inches_x(x), ux(x, unit) (convert_x()) and mm_y(y), cm_y(y), inch_y(y) / inches_y(y), uy(y, unit) (convert_y()): convert physical lengths into data units along the x- or y-axis of the current cell (or a specified sector_index, track_index). mm_x(2) mm_x(1, sector_index="a", track_index=1) mm_y(2) mm_y(1, sector_index="a", track_index=1) Because cell arc width varies from the bottom radius to the top radius of a track, *_x() helpers also accept an h argument (y position in data coordinates, defaulting to ycenter): mm_x(2, h=0.8) Here is a concrete example combining mm_h(), cm_h(), inch_h(), mm_x(), cm_x(), and cm_y(): import math import numpy as np from circlize_py import CELL_META, circos, cm_h, cm_x, cm_y, inch_h, mm_h, mm_x rng = np.random.default_rng(77) sectors = list("abcdefghij") xlim = np.column_stack([np.zeros(10), rng.uniform(0.5, 1.5, size=10)]) circos.par(cell_padding=[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0], track_margin=[0.0, 0.0]) circos.initialize(sectors, xlim=xlim) circos.track( ylim=[0.0, 1.0], track_height=mm_h(5), panel_fun=lambda x, y: circos.lines([0.0, mm_x(5)], [0.5, 0.5], col="blue"), ) circos.track( ylim=[0.0, 1.0], track_height=cm_h(1), track_margin=[0.0, mm_h(2)], panel_fun=lambda x, y: circos.lines([CELL_META.xcenter, CELL_META.xcenter], [0.0, cm_y(1)], col="red"), ) circos.track( ylim=[0.0, 1.0], track_height=inch_h(1), track_margin=[0.0, mm_h(5)], panel_fun=lambda x, y: circos.lines( [0.0, cm_x(math.sqrt(2) / 2.0)], [0.0, cm_y(math.sqrt(2) / 2.0)], col="orange", ), ) circos.clear() Setting absolute units

title:
2.8.3 circos.info() and
circos.clear()
text: Call circos.info() at any point to inspect initialized sectors, tracks, and individual cell coordinates: sectors = ["a", "b", "c"] circos.initialize(sectors, xlim=[1, 2]) circos.info() circos.track(ylim=[0, 1]) circos.info(sector_index="a", track_index=1) circos.clear() All your sectors: ['a', 'b', 'c'] No track has been created Your current sector.index is a --- sector index: 'a' track index: 1 xlim: [1.0, 2.0] ylim: [0.0, 1.0] cell.xlim: [0.9914529914529915, 2.0085470085470085] cell.ylim: [-0.09999999999999999, 1.1] xplot (degree): [360.0, 241.0] yplot (radius): [0.79, 0.99] cell.width (degree): 119.0 cell.height (radius): 0.2 track.margin: [0.01, 0.01] cell.padding: [0.02, 1.0, 0.02, 1.0] Your current sector.index is c Your current track.index is 1 Calling circos.info(plot=True) draws sector:track labels directly inside every cell—handy for debugging complex multi-track layouts. Always finish each circular figure with circos.clear() so global parameters do not leak into subsequent plots.

title: 2.9 Set gaps between tracks
text: set_track_gap() adjusts track_margin cleanly to place an exact radial gap between consecutive tracks using physical units such as mm_h() or cm_h(): from circlize_py import circos, cm_h, mm_h, set_track_gap circos.initialize(list("abcdefghij"), xlim=[0, 1]) circos.track(ylim=[0, 1]) set_track_gap(mm_h(2)) # 2 mm gap before next track circos.track(ylim=[0, 1]) set_track_gap(cm_h(0.5)) # 0.5 cm gap before next track circos.track(ylim=[0, 1]) circos.clear() Setting gaps between tracks

title: 3 Graphics
text: This chapter introduces the low-level and track-level functions that add visual elements inside circular cells. Most mirror standard Matplotlib or R base graphics primitives (points, lines, segments, rect, polygon, text, axis), extended with polar-aware geometry. Every low-level function accepts sector_index and track_index to target a specific cell. By default, graphics are drawn into the “current” sector and track, so calling them inside panel_fun is the cleanest pattern. Outside panel_fun, supply sector_index and track_index explicitly: circos.track( ..., panel_fun=lambda x, y: circos.points(x, y), ) circos.points(x, y, sector_index="a", track_index=1) We also cover links (circos.link()), sector/track highlighting (draw.sector(), highlight.sector()), and combining circlize-py plots with Matplotlib Axes annotations.

title: 3.1 Setting colors
text: circlize-py provides utilities for continuous color mapping, inverse value lookup, transparency adjustment, and distinct random color generation (in addition to supporting all 657 R named colors, R palette indices 1..8, hex #RRGGBB / #RRGGBBAA, and Matplotlib color specs). colorRamp2() (or color_ramp2()) builds a continuous color-mapping callable by linearly interpolating between break points in perceptual color space ("LAB" by default, plus "RGB", "sRGB", "XYZ", "LUV", and "HLS"). Values outside the break range clamp to the endpoints: import numpy as np from circlize_py import colorRamp2 col_fun = colorRamp2([-2, 0, 2], ["blue", "white", "red"]) print(col_fun(np.arange(-5, 2, 1))) ['#0000FFFF' '#0000FFFF' '#0000FFFF' '#0000FFFF' '#B38BFFFF' '#FFFFFFFF' '#FF9E81FF'] add_transparency() adjusts color opacity with transparency in [0, 1] (0 = opaque, 1 = fully transparent): from circlize_py import add_transparency add_transparency("#FF0000", 0.5) # '#FF000080' rand_color() implements the randomColor.js palette generator with optional hue, luminosity, transparency, friendly, and seed arguments: import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np from circlize_py import rand_color fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 5.8)) xs = np.arange(1, 11) specs = [ (1, dict(luminosity="random")), (2, dict(luminosity="bright")), (3, dict(luminosity="light")), (4, dict(luminosity="dark")), (5, dict(hue="red", luminosity="bright")), (6, dict(hue="green", luminosity="bright")), (7, dict(hue="blue", luminosity="bright")), (8, dict(hue="monochrome", luminosity="bright")), ] for y_row, kw in specs: ax.scatter(xs, np.repeat(y_row, 10), s=520, c=rand_color(10, **kw)) ax.axis("off") Random color palettes generated by rand_color() col2value() performs the inverse transformation—recovering approximate numeric values from colors generated by a colorRamp2() function: from circlize_py import col2value, colorRamp2 col_fun = colorRamp2([-2, 0, 2], ["blue", "white", "red"]) value = np.round(np.arange(-2.0, 2.01, 0.2), 2) cols = col_fun(value) print(np.round(col2value(cols, col_fun=col_fun), 3)) [-2. -1.796 -1.595 -1.391 -1.19 -0.987 -0.785 -0.586 -0.39 -0.199 -0. 0.176 0.359 0.545 0.743 0.942 1.151 1.36 1.575 1.786 2. ]

title: 3.2 Points
text: circos.points() adds points inside a cell using R-compatible pch marker codes (0..25 or Matplotlib marker strings), col, bg, and cex: circos.points(x, y) circos.points(x, y, sector_index="a", track_index=1) circos.points(x, y, pch=16, col="red", cex=0.8) Its track-level companion circos.trackPoints() (or circos_track_points()) splits x and y by sectors and draws points across all cells on a track simultaneously: circos.track(...) circos.trackPoints(sectors, x, y) While convenient for simple point overlays, circos.points() inside panel_fun is recommended because it composes cleanly with other primitives: circos.track(sectors, x=x, y=y, panel_fun=lambda xv, yv: circos.points(xv, yv)) Other primitives also provide circos.track*() batch helpers (circos.trackLines(), circos.trackText()) with the same calling pattern.

title: 3.3 Lines
text: circos.lines() draws line paths inside a cell. Setting area=True fills the region between the curve and baseline (which can be "bottom", "top", or a numeric y-coordinate); col sets the line color (or fill color when area=True), and border controls the polygon outline when area=True. When type="h", vertical needles are drawn from baseline to each y value, and col, lwd, and lty can be passed as sequences matching x. Supported type options ("l", "o", "h", "s") and area / baseline combinations are illustrated below: Line styles and areas supported in circos.lines() Straight lines in data coordinates curve into circular arcs on the circle by subdividing each segment according to circos.par("unit.circle.segments"), where each arc piece has maximum length 2 * pi / unit_circle_segments. For purely radial lines (or when straight chord segments are preferred for performance), pass straight=True: Transformation of straight lines into curves in the circle Common call patterns for circos.lines(): circos.lines(x, y) circos.lines(x, y, sector_index="a", track_index=1) circos.lines(x, y, col="red", lwd=1.5, lty=2, type="l", straight=False) circos.lines(x, y, col="#CCCCCC", area=True, baseline="bottom", border="black")

title: 3.4 Segments
text: circos.segments() draws individual line segments from (x0, y0) to (x1, y1). Pass straight=True for straight chord segments or radial lines: circos.segments(x0, y0, x1, y1) circos.segments(x0, y0, x1, y1, straight=True) import numpy as np from circlize_py import circos circos.initialize(list("abcdefgh"), xlim=[0.0, 1.0]) def panel_seg(x, y): vals = np.array([0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8]) circos.segments(vals, 0.1, vals, 0.9) circos.segments(0.1, vals, 0.9, vals) circos.track(ylim=[0.0, 1.0], track_height=0.3, panel_fun=panel_seg) circos.clear() Draw segments

title: 3.5 Text
text: circos.text() draws labels in a cell with seven circularly aware facing modes: "inside", "outside", "clockwise", "reverse.clockwise", "downward", "bending.inside", and "bending.outside". Note that "bending.inside" and "bending.outside" bend single-line strings along the arc (split multi-line bent labels into separate circos.text() calls). Text facings Common usages of circos.text(): circos.text(x, y, labels) circos.text(x, y, labels, sector_index="a", track_index=1) circos.text(x, y, labels, facing="inside", nice_facing=True, adj=[0.5, 0.5], cex=1.0, col="black", font=1) Without nice_facing=True (niceFacing=True), labels in the lower or left halves of the circle can appear upside down. Enabling nice_facing=True automatically flips text orientation—and mirrors adj consistently—for "inside", "outside", "clockwise", "reverse.clockwise", "bending.inside", and "bending.outside" so every label stays upright and readable: Human-readable text facing adj adjusts horizontal and vertical alignment in the rotated text frame. When offsetting along the circular axis in degrees, wrap the offset with degree() from circlize_py: from circlize_py import degree circos.text(x, y, labels, adj=[0.0, degree(5)], facing="clockwise") To apply physical offsets in data coordinates, add mm_x() / mm_y() (or cm_x() / cm_y()): circos.text(x + mm_x(2), y + mm_y(2), labels)

title: 3.6 Rectangles and polygons
text: circos.rect() maps Cartesian rectangles [xleft, xright] x [ybottom, ytop] onto circular cells whose top and bottom edges follow circular arcs. All coordinate and style arguments are vectorized: circos.rect(xleft, ybottom, xright, ytop) circos.rect(xleft, ybottom, xright, ytop, sector_index="a", track_index=1) circos.rect(xleft, ybottom, xright, ytop, col="skyblue", border="black", lty=1, lwd=1.0) circos.polygon() draws closed polygons from (x, y) vertices in data coordinates (subdividing edges into smooth circular arcs): circos.polygon(x, y) circos.polygon(x, y, col="#CCCCCC", border=None, lty=1, lwd=1.0) The figure below uses circos.polygon() to shade a pointwise standard-error confidence ribbon around a LOESS-smoothed trend line in each sector: Area of standard deviation around a smoothed line

title: 3.7 Axes
text: circos.axis() (alias circos.xaxis()) adds circular x-axes at h="top", h="bottom", or any numeric y coordinate inside a cell. Major tick positions (major_at) and labels (labels) exceeding [xlim[0], xlim[1]] are clipped automatically, edge labels are nudged inward when labels_pos_adjust=True, and label orientation defaults to labels_nice_facing=True. In the eight-sector showcase below: a: Automatic major ticks and default settings (h="top", direction="outside"). b: Inward ticks (direction="inside") with labels_facing="outside". c: Axis positioned along h="bottom". d: Bottom axis with inward ticks (direction="inside") and labels_facing="reverse.clockwise". e: Custom major_at=[1, 3, 5, 7, 9] placed midway at h=5. f: Custom string labels (labels=["a", "c", "e", "g", "f"]) with minor_ticks=0. g: Hidden ticks (major_tick=False) with labels_facing="reverse.clockwise". h: minor_ticks=2, longer major ticks via major_tick_length=mm_y(5), and labels_facing="clockwise". X-axes Common call signatures for circos.axis(): circos.axis(h="top") circos.axis(h="top", sector_index="a", track_index=1) circos.axis(h=5, major_at=[1, 3, 5, 7, 9], labels=True, major_tick=True, direction="outside") circos.axis( h=2, major_at=[1, 3, 5, 7, 9], labels=["a1", "c1", "e1", "g1", "f1"], minor_ticks=2, major_tick_length=mm_y(5), labels_cex=0.8, labels_facing="clockwise", ) Radial y-axes are drawn with circos.yaxis() on either the "left" or "right" border of a cell. Make sure gap_degree / gap_after in circos.par() leaves enough room between neighboring sectors for y-axis labels: circos.yaxis(side="left") circos.yaxis(side="right", at=[0, 5, 10], labels=["low", "mid", "high"], sector_index="e", track_index=1) Y-axes

title:
3.8 Barplots, boxplots and
violin plots
text: circos.barplot(), circos.boxplot(), and circos.violin() position bars, boxes, or violins along explicit x-axis coordinates (pos), so choose xlim in circos.initialize() to frame all positions cleanly. circos.barplot() accepts a 1D vector (including signed values extending above and below 0) or a 2D array/DataFrame (drawing stacked bars by column): import numpy as np from circlize_py import circos rng = np.random.default_rng(11) pos = np.arange(1, 11) - 0.5 # Left: 1D positive & signed barplots circos.initialize(list("abcd"), xlim=[0.0, 10.0]) circos.track( ylim=[0.0, 1.0], panel_fun=lambda x, y: circos.barplot(rng.uniform(0, 1, size=10), pos, col=list(range(1, 11))), ) def panel_signed(x, y): val = rng.uniform(-1, 1, size=10) circos.barplot(val, pos, col=[2 if v > 0 else 3 for v in val]) circos.track(ylim=[-1.0, 1.0], panel_fun=panel_signed) circos.clear() # Right: 2D stacked barplot circos.initialize(list("abcd"), xlim=[0.0, 10.0]) circos.track( ylim=[0.0, 4.0], panel_fun=lambda x, y: circos.barplot(rng.uniform(0, 1, size=(10, 4)), pos, col=[2, 3, 4, 5]), ) circos.clear() Circular barplots circos.boxplot() can draw individual boxes one at a time from 1D arrays, or render a batch of boxes from a list of arrays or a 2D matrix/DataFrame (by columns): # One-by-one inside panel_fun circos.initialize(list("abcd"), xlim=[0.0, 10.0]) circos.track( ylim=[0.0, 1.0], panel_fun=lambda x, y: [circos.boxplot(rng.uniform(0, 1, size=10), p) for p in np.arange(0.5, 10.0, 1.0)], ) circos.clear() # Batch list of vectors circos.initialize(list("abcd"), xlim=[0.0, 10.0]) circos.track( ylim=[0.0, 1.0], panel_fun=lambda x, y: circos.boxplot( [rng.uniform(0, 1, size=10) for _ in range(10)], np.arange(1, 11) - 0.5, col=list(range(1, 11)), ), ) circos.clear() Circular boxplots circos.violin() shares the same single-vector and batch list/matrix interface, estimating kernel density per distribution. Pass max_density explicitly when normalizing violin widths consistently across separate calls: circos.initialize(list("abcd"), xlim=[0.0, 10.0]) circos.track( ylim=[0.0, 1.0], panel_fun=lambda x, y: [circos.violin(rng.uniform(0, 1, size=10), p) for p in np.arange(0.5, 10.0, 1.0)], ) circos.clear() circos.initialize(list("abcd"), xlim=[0.0, 10.0]) circos.track( ylim=[0.0, 1.0], panel_fun=lambda x, y: circos.violin( [rng.uniform(0, 1, size=10) for _ in range(10)], np.arange(1, 11) - 0.5, col=list(range(1, 11)), ), ) circos.clear() Circular violin plots

title: 3.9 Circular arrows
text: circos.arrow() draws curved arrows running parallel to a track between x1 and x2 centered radially at y. width, arrow_head_width, and arrow_head_length are given in cell data units (and can use mm_x(), cm_x(), mm_y()). tail toggles between "normal" and "point", and setting arrow_position="start" reverses the pointing direction: from circlize_py import CELL_META, circos, cm_x, rand_color cols = rand_color(4, seed=44) tails = ["point", "normal", "point", "normal"] circos.initialize(list("abcd"), xlim=[0.0, 1.0]) circos.track( ylim=[0.0, 1.0], bg_border=None, track_height=0.4, panel_fun=lambda x, y: circos.arrow( x1=0.0, x2=1.0, y=0.5, width=0.4, arrow_head_width=0.6, arrow_head_length=cm_x(1.0), col=cols[CELL_META.sector_numeric_index - 1], tail=tails[CELL_META.sector_numeric_index - 1], arrow_position="end", # or "start" ), ) circos.clear() Circular arrows Circular arrows are natural for cyclic processes such as the eukaryotic cell cycle (with sector widths proportional to phase durations) or strand orientation along circular mitochondrial and plasmid genomes (using arrow_position="start" for reverse-strand features): import numpy as np import pandas as pd from circlize_py import CELL_META, circos, cm_x phases = ["G1", "S", "G2", "M"] cell_cycle = pd.DataFrame( { "phase": pd.Categorical(phases, categories=phases, ordered=True), "hour": [11.0, 8.0, 4.0, 1.0], } ) colors = ["#66C2A5", "#FC8D62", "#8DA0CB", "#E78AC3"] circos.par(start_degree=90, points_overflow_warning=False) xlim = np.column_stack([np.zeros(4), cell_cycle["hour"].to_numpy()]) circos.initialize(cell_cycle["phase"], xlim=xlim) def panel_cycle(x, y): circos.arrow( CELL_META.xlim[0], CELL_META.xlim[1], arrow_head_width=CELL_META.yrange * 0.8, arrow_head_length=cm_x(0.5), col=colors[CELL_META.sector_numeric_index - 1], ) circos.text(CELL_META.xcenter, CELL_META.ycenter, CELL_META.sector_index, facing="downward") circos.axis(h=1.0, major_at=np.arange(0, int(round(CELL_META.xlim[1])) + 1), minor_ticks=1, labels_cex=0.6) circos.track(ylim=[0.0, 1.0], bg_border=None, track_height=0.3, panel_fun=panel_cycle) circos.clear() Cell cycle

title: 3.10 Labels
text: circos.labels() adds two tracks—one for connector segments and one for radially aligned text labels—while automatically repelling crowded neighboring labels. Set side="inside" (default) to place labels inward of existing tracks, or side="outside" to place them outward: # Inside labels circos.initialize(sectors=list("abcdefgh"), xlim=[0.0, 1.0]) circos.track(ylim=[0.0, 1.0]) circos.labels(["a", "a", "b", "b"], x=[0.1, 0.12, 0.4, 0.6], labels=["0.1", "0.12", "0.4", "0.6"]) circos.clear() # Outside labels (call before inner tracks) circos.initialize(sectors=list("abcdefgh"), xlim=[0.0, 1.0]) circos.labels(["a", "a", "b", "b"], x=[0.1, 0.12, 0.4, 0.6], labels=["0.1", "0.12", "0.4", "0.6"], side="outside") circos.track(ylim=[0.0, 1.0]) circos.clear() Label track

title: 3.11 Raster image
text: circos.raster() places a NumPy image array, PIL Image, or image file path inside a cell with automatic rotation matching facing ("inside", "outside", "reverse.clockwise", "clockwise", "downward") and nice_facing. For flat rotated images, pass physical dimensions such as width="1cm" or height="20mm"; if only one dimension is specified, the other preserves the image aspect ratio: from circlize_py import CELL_META, circos, load_extdata img = load_extdata("Rlogo.png") circos.par(start_degree=90) circos.initialize(list("abcde"), xlim=[0.0, 1.0]) facings = ["inside", "outside", "reverse.clockwise", "clockwise", "downward"] def panel_logo(x, y): f = facings[CELL_META.sector_numeric_index - 1] circos.raster(img, CELL_META.xcenter, CELL_META.ycenter, width="1cm", facing=f) circos.text(CELL_META.xcenter, CELL_META.ycenter, f, facing="inside", nice_facing=True, cex=0.85) circos.track(ylim=[0.0, 1.0], panel_fun=panel_logo) circos.clear() Five facings of a raster image Setting facing="bending.inside" or "bending.outside" warps the raster directly onto the polar grid by rendering pixels as circular rectangles in data coordinates (width and height are mandatory in data units; scaling < 1.0 downsamples large rasters for faster plotting). Below, the 32 bundled Keith Haring tiles from load_extdata("doodle") fill two concentric tracks: from circlize_py import CELL_META, circos, load_extdata imgs = load_extdata("doodle") circos.par(cell_padding=[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) circos.initialize(list("abcdefghijklmnop"), xlim=[0.0, 1.0]) circos.track( ylim=[0.0, 1.0], track_height=0.25, bg_border=None, panel_fun=lambda x, y: circos.raster( imgs[CELL_META.sector_numeric_index - 1], CELL_META.xcenter, CELL_META.ycenter, width=CELL_META.xrange, height=CELL_META.yrange, facing="bending.inside", scaling=0.5, ), ) circos.track( ylim=[0.0, 1.0], track_height=0.25, bg_border=None, panel_fun=lambda x, y: circos.raster( imgs[CELL_META.sector_numeric_index + 15], CELL_META.xcenter, CELL_META.ycenter, width=CELL_META.xrange, height=CELL_META.yrange, facing="bending.inside", scaling=0.5, ), ) circos.clear() Fill raster images to cells

title: 3.12 Links
text: Links and ribbons connect pairs of positions or intervals across sectors inside the circle via circos.link(). Its four required arguments are (sector_index1, point1, sector_index2, point2). Single scalar endpoints produce curved lines, whereas length-2 intervals [start, end] produce ribbons: circos.link(sector_index1, 0, sector_index2, 0) circos.link(sector_index1, [0, 1], sector_index2, 0) circos.link(sector_index1, [0, 1], sector_index2, [1, 2]) circos.link(sector_index1, [0, 1], sector_index2, 0, col="red", lwd=1.5, lty=2, border="blue") sectors = list("abcdefgh") circos.par(points_overflow_warning=False) circos.initialize(sectors, xlim=[0.0, 10.0]) circos.track(sectors, ylim=[0.0, 1.0], bg_col="grey", bg_border=None, track_height=0.05) circos.link("a", 5, "c", 5, border="black") circos.link("b", 5, "d", [4, 6], border="black") circos.link("a", [2, 3], "f", [4, 6], border="black") circos.link("e", [2, 3], "g", 5, border="black") circos.clear() Different types of links Radial attachment positions default to just inside the innermost track, and can be overridden uniformly via rou or independently via rou1 and rou2: circos.link("a", 5, "c", 5, rou2=0.5, border="black") circos.link("b", 5, "d", [4, 6], rou2=0.5, border="black") circos.link("a", [2, 3], "f", [4, 6], rou2=0.5, border="black") Positions of link ends Link arch depth is controlled by h (top border) and h2 (bottom border). Although circlize-py computes sensible defaults automatically, very asymmetric or closely spaced ribbons can self-intersect unless h and h2 are set manually: circos.link("a", 10, "b", [1, 9], border="black") circos.link("c", 10, "d", [1, 9], h=0.5, h2=0.2, border="black") Adjust link heights When drawing many links at once, h_ratio (in [0, 1], default 0.5) systematically scales how deeply curves arch toward the center of the circle: Adjust link heights with h_ratio Because link curves are rational quadratic Bézier splines, w and w2 adjust the Bézier control-point weight (w > 1 pulls sharper toward the center, w < 0 arches outward): Different link shapes When both interval endpoints belong to the same sector and overlap, the ribbon degenerates cleanly into a rounded “hill”: Link as a hill Directionality is added with directional (0 = none, 1 = end 1 to end 2, -1 = end 2 to end 1, 2 = bidirectional). Line links get terminal arrowheads, while ribbons receive a centered directional arrow—or become a shaped arrow ribbon when arr_type="big.arrow": circos.link("a", 5, "b", 5, directional=1, arr_length=0.2) circos.link("c", [3, 7], "d", [3, 7], directional=1, arr_col="white", arr_length=0.2) circos.link("e", [4, 6], "f", [4, 6], directional=1, arr_type="big.arrow", arr_length=0.04) Links with arrows

title: 3.13 Highlight sectors and tracks
text: draw.sector() (or draw_sector()) draws standalone circular wedges, rings, or circles in polar coordinates on the canvas: draw.sector(start_degree, end_degree, rou1=1.0, rou2=None, center=(0, 0), clock_wise=True, col=None, border="black", lwd=1.0, lty=1) import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from circlize_py import draw fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 5.4)) ax.set_xlim(-1.05, 1.05) ax.set_ylim(-1.05, 1.05) ax.set_aspect("equal") ax.axis("off") draw.sector(20, 0, ax=ax) draw.sector(30, 60, rou1=0.8, rou2=0.5, clock_wise=False, col="#FF000080", ax=ax) draw.sector(350, 1000, col="#00FF0080", border=None, ax=ax) draw.sector(0, 180, rou1=0.25, center=(-0.5, 0.5), border=2, lwd=2, lty=2, ax=ax) draw.sector(0, 360, rou1=0.7, rou2=0.6, col="#0000FF80", ax=ax) General usage of draw.sector() Combining draw.sector() with get_cell_meta_data() and circlize() lets you highlight arbitrary sectors, full tracks, cell blocks, or sub-regions inside a cell: from circlize_py import circos, circlize, draw, get_cell_meta_data sectors = list("abcdefgh") circos.initialize(sectors, xlim=[0.0, 1.0]) for _ in range(3): circos.track(ylim=[0.0, 1.0]) circos.info(plot=True) # Highlight sector "a" draw.sector( get_cell_meta_data("cell.start.degree", sector_index="a"), get_cell_meta_data("cell.end.degree", sector_index="a"), rou1=get_cell_meta_data("cell.top.radius", track_index=1), col="#FF000040", ) # Highlight track 1 draw.sector( 0, 360, rou1=get_cell_meta_data("cell.top.radius", track_index=1), rou2=get_cell_meta_data("cell.bottom.radius", track_index=1), col="#00FF0040", ) # Highlight tracks 2 & 3 across sectors "e" and "f" draw.sector( get_cell_meta_data("cell.start.degree", sector_index="e"), get_cell_meta_data("cell.end.degree", sector_index="f"), rou1=get_cell_meta_data("cell.top.radius", track_index=2), rou2=get_cell_meta_data("cell.bottom.radius", track_index=3), col="#0000FF40", ) # Highlight sub-region [0.2, 0.8] x [0.2, 0.8] inside cell h:2 pos = circlize([0.2, 0.8], [0.2, 0.8], sector_index="h", track_index=2) draw.sector(pos[0, "theta"], pos[1, "theta"], pos[0, "rou"], pos[1, "rou"], clock_wise=True, col="#00FFFF40") circos.clear() Highlight sectors and tracks When highlighting whole cells or contiguous sector/track blocks, highlight.sector() (or highlight_sector()) eliminates manual degree lookups, supports fractional padding=[bottom, left, top, right] (or literal data units via I(...)), and can place curved or rotated annotation text with text and text_vjust (including physical strings like "6mm"): from circlize_py import circos, highlight sectors = list("abcdefgh") circos.initialize(sectors, xlim=[0.0, 1.0]) for _ in range(4): circos.track(ylim=[0.0, 1.0]) circos.info(plot=True) highlight.sector( ["a", "h"], track_index=1, text="a and h belong to a same group", facing="bending.inside", nice_facing=True, text_vjust="6mm", cex=0.8, ) highlight.sector("c", col="#00FF0040") highlight.sector("d", col=None, border="red", lwd=2) highlight.sector("e", col="#0000FF40", track_index=[2, 3]) highlight.sector(["f", "g"], col=None, border="green", lwd=2, track_index=[2, 3], padding=[0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1]) highlight.sector(sectors, col="#FFFF0040", track_index=4) circos.clear() Highlight sectors with highlight.sector()

title:
3.14 Work together with Matplotlib
Axes
text: Because circlize-py renders directly onto a Matplotlib Axes, you can freely combine circular plots with standard Matplotlib annotations—titles, center labels, legends, or custom artists—and use polar2Cartesian(circlize(...)) whenever you want to map cell data coordinates onto canvas coordinates: import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np from matplotlib.lines import Line2D from circlize_py import circos fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 6.0), dpi=140) sectors = list("abcd") circos.initialize(sectors, xlim=[0.0, 1.0], ax=ax) vals = np.arange(1, 21) / 20.0 circos.track(ylim=[0.0, 1.0], panel_fun=lambda x, y: circos.points(vals, vals)) ax.text(0.0, 0.0, "This is\nthe center", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=14) handle = Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", linestyle="None", markerfacecolor="none", markeredgecolor="black", markersize=6) ax.legend([handle], ["This is the legend"], loc="lower left", frameon=True, fontsize=9) ax.set_title("This is the title", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", pad=10) circos.clear() Work with Matplotlib Axes functions

title: 4 Legends
text: circlize provides complete freedom for users to design custom circular graphics through panel_fun callbacks. However, because circlize renders arbitrary user-supplied primitives rather than owning a high-level plot grammar, it does not automatically generate legends for tracks or links. In circlize-py, every circular plot is drawn onto a standard Matplotlib Axes. That means legends can be built and arranged seamlessly using Matplotlib’s native fig.legend(), fig.colorbar(), GridSpec, and explicit figure axes—requiring only a few lines of Python. In the book’s figure helper module (_common.py), two thin wrappers—add_discrete_legend() and add_colorbar()—illustrate this pattern directly on top of Matplotlib’s Line2D/Patch artists and ScalarMappable colorbars. As a running example, we construct a circular plot with two tracks and interior links. The first track plots two groups of points, the second track plots two groups of lines, and the links use a continuous ColorRamp2 mapping. We wrap the circular plot in a reusable function draw_example_circle() so we can pair it with several legend layouts. import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from circlize import add_transparency, circos, color_ramp2 col_fun = color_ramp2([-2.0, 0.0, 2.0], ["green", "yellow", "red"]) def draw_example_circle(seed: int = 12345) -> None: rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) sectors = list("abcdefghij") circos.initialize(sectors, xlim=(0.0, 1.0)) def panel_track1(x, y): circos.points(rng.uniform(size=20), rng.uniform(size=20), cex=0.5, pch=16, col=2) circos.points(rng.uniform(size=20), rng.uniform(size=20), cex=0.5, pch=16, col=3) circos.track(ylim=(0.0, 1.0), panel_fun=panel_track1) def panel_track2(x, y): circos.lines(np.sort(rng.uniform(size=20)), rng.uniform(size=20), col=4) circos.lines(np.sort(rng.uniform(size=20)), rng.uniform(size=20), col=5) circos.track(ylim=(0.0, 1.0), panel_fun=panel_track2) for _ in range(10): s1 = str(rng.choice(sectors)) s2 = str(rng.choice(sectors)) p1 = np.sort(rng.uniform(size=10))[:2] p2 = np.sort(rng.uniform(size=10))[:2] # Pass transparency=0.5 explicitly to match semi-transparent ribbons col = add_transparency(col_fun(float(rng.normal())), transparency=0.5) circos.link(s1, p1, s2, p2, col=col) circos.clear()

title:
4.1 Building discrete and continuous
legends with Matplotlib
text: To render legends alongside any circlize-py figure: Discrete point, line, or patch legends (fig.legend / add_discrete_legend): Build proxy matplotlib.lines.Line2D or matplotlib.patches.Patch handles using color_to_hex() (so R palette indices like 2–5 and R color names resolve identically to circlize-py tracks), and attach them with fig.legend(...). Calling fig.legend() multiple times appends independent legend boxes to the figure without replacing earlier legends (whereas calling ax.legend() repeatedly on a single Axes replaces the previous legend unless ax.add_artist() is used). Continuous colorbars (fig.colorbar / add_colorbar): Sample a ColorRamp2 object across [vmin, vmax] into a Matplotlib LinearSegmentedColormap (colorramp_to_cmap()), wrap it in matplotlib.cm.ScalarMappable(norm=Normalize(vmin, vmax), cmap=cmap), and draw it into a dedicated axes box [left, bottom, width, height] via fig.colorbar(sm, cax=cax). from matplotlib.cm import ScalarMappable from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap, Normalize from matplotlib.lines import Line2D from circlize import color_to_hex def make_discrete_handles(items, kind="point"): handles = [] for label, color in items: hex_col = color_to_hex(color, include_alpha=True) if kind == "point": handles.append( Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", linestyle="None", markerfacecolor=hex_col, markeredgecolor=hex_col, markersize=6.0, label=label) ) elif kind == "line": handles.append(Line2D([0], [0], color=hex_col, lw=2.0, label=label)) return handles def colorramp_to_cmap(col_fun, vmin, vmax, n=256): vals = np.linspace(vmin, vmax, n) cols = [color_to_hex(col_fun(float(v)), include_alpha=True) for v in vals] return LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("circlize_ramp", cols, N=n)

title: 4.2 Overlaying legends on the figure canvas
text: Because fig.legend() and fig.add_axes() use normalized figure coordinates ([0, 1] × [0, 1]), legends can be placed directly in the corners of the circular canvas. The helper add_discrete_legend() wraps proxy handle creation and fig.legend(), while add_colorbar() creates a small colorbar axes at rect=[left, bottom, width, height]. fig = plt.figure(figsize=(5.0, 5.0), dpi=140, facecolor="white") ax = fig.add_axes([0.04, 0.04, 0.92, 0.92]) plt.sca(ax) draw_example_circle() add_discrete_legend( fig, [("label1", 2), ("label2", 3)], kind="point", title="Track1", loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.02, 0.43), ) add_discrete_legend( fig, [("label3", 4), ("label4", 5)], kind="line", title="Track2", loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.02, 0.27), ) add_colorbar( fig, col_fun, vmin=-2.0, vmax=2.0, rect=[0.04, 0.04, 0.032, 0.19], title="Links", ticks=[-2, -1, 0, 1, 2], ) Directly overlaid corner legends on the circular plot. As the stacked corner legends demonstrate, overlaying multiple legends directly on a compact square canvas leaves them overlapping the outer circular tracks. One quick mitigation on a wider canvas is to split the legends across different corners—for example, placing the discrete track legends in the lower-left corner and the continuous link colorbar in the lower-right corner. fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.2, 5.0), dpi=140, facecolor="white") ax = fig.add_axes([0.06, 0.04, 0.88, 0.92]) plt.sca(ax) draw_example_circle() add_discrete_legend( fig, [("label1", 2), ("label2", 3)], kind="point", title="Track1", loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.02, 0.19), ) add_discrete_legend( fig, [("label3", 4), ("label4", 5)], kind="line", title="Track2", loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.02, 0.03), ) add_colorbar( fig, col_fun, vmin=-2.0, vmax=2.0, rect=[0.89, 0.05, 0.028, 0.22], title="Links", ticks=[-2, -1, 0, 1, 2], ) Legends split across the bottom-left and bottom-right corners.

title:
4.3 Partitioning space with
GridSpec
text: Corner placement still breaks down when legends are tall or numerous. The cleanest, most reliable solution is to partition the Matplotlib figure with fig.add_gridspec() so the circular plot occupies one region and the legends live in their own non-overlapping panel. First, use a 1 × 2 GridSpec (width_ratios=[4.2, 1.2]) to reserve a dedicated right-side legend column. Activate the left subplot with plt.sca(ax_circ) before calling draw_example_circle(), then read the right subplot’s normalized figure box (pos = ax_leg.get_position()) to anchor the discrete legends and colorbar axes cleanly inside the right column: fig = plt.figure(figsize=(7.0, 5.2), dpi=140, facecolor="white") gs = fig.add_gridspec( 1, 2, width_ratios=[4.2, 1.2], left=0.02, right=0.96, top=0.97, bottom=0.03, wspace=0.04, ) ax_circ = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0]) plt.sca(ax_circ) draw_example_circle() ax_leg = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 1]) ax_leg.set_axis_off() pos = ax_leg.get_position() add_discrete_legend( fig, [("label1", 2), ("label2", 3)], kind="point", title="Track1", loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(pos.x0, pos.y0 + 0.78 * pos.height), ) add_discrete_legend( fig, [("label3", 4), ("label4", 5)], kind="line", title="Track2", loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(pos.x0, pos.y0 + 0.59 * pos.height), ) add_colorbar( fig, col_fun, vmin=-2.0, vmax=2.0, rect=[pos.x0 + 0.012, pos.y0 + 0.16 * pos.height, 0.025, 0.22 * pos.height], title="Links", ticks=[-2, -1, 0, 1, 2], ) Circular plot with a dedicated right-side legend column built via GridSpec. Legends can just as easily sit below the circular plot by switching to a 2 × 1 GridSpec (height_ratios=[4.3, 1.0]), passing ncol=2 to add_discrete_legend(), and setting orientation="horizontal" on add_colorbar(): fig = plt.figure(figsize=(5.6, 6.4), dpi=140, facecolor="white") gs = fig.add_gridspec( 2, 1, height_ratios=[4.3, 1.0], left=0.03, right=0.97, top=0.98, bottom=0.04, hspace=0.03, ) ax_circ = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0]) plt.sca(ax_circ) draw_example_circle() ax_leg = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 0]) ax_leg.set_axis_off() pos = ax_leg.get_position() add_discrete_legend( fig, [("label1", 2), ("label2", 3)], kind="point", title="Track1", ncol=2, loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(pos.x0 + 0.02 * pos.width, pos.y0 + 0.50 * pos.height), ) add_discrete_legend( fig, [("label3", 4), ("label4", 5)], kind="line", title="Track2", ncol=2, loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(pos.x0 + 0.34 * pos.width, pos.y0 + 0.50 * pos.height), ) add_colorbar( fig, col_fun, vmin=-2.0, vmax=2.0, rect=[pos.x0 + 0.68 * pos.width, pos.y0 + 0.42 * pos.height, 0.28 * pos.width, 0.16 * pos.height], title="Links", ticks=[-2, -1, 0, 1, 2], orientation="horizontal", ) Circular plot with horizontal legends placed in a dedicated bottom row via GridSpec. See the circos.heatmap() chapter for an extended multi-track example combining eight discrete and continuous legends alongside a complex circular heatmap.

title: 5 Implement high-level circular plots
text: In this chapter, we demonstrate several examples that combine low-level graphic primitives to construct specialized high-level circular visualizations.

title: 5.1 Circular barplots
text: circlize-py already provides circos.barplot() for vertical radial bars. Here we construct a different style—concentric horizontal bars arranged inside a single sector and track (you could equivalently place them into nine separate tracks with almost identical code). import numpy as np import matplotlib.colors as mcolors import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from circlize import CELL_META, circos, mm_x rng = np.random.default_rng(123) category = [f"category_{i}" for i in range(1, 10)] percent = np.sort(rng.integers(40, 81, size=9)) cmap = plt.get_cmap("rainbow") color = [mcolors.to_hex(cmap(v)) for v in np.linspace(1.0, 0.0, len(percent))] circos.par(start_degree=90, cell_padding=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0), points_overflow_warning=False) circos.initialize(["a"], xlim=(0.0, 100.0)) # "a" creates one single sector def panel_bar(x, y): xlim = CELL_META.xlim ys = np.arange(1, 10, dtype=float) circos.segments(np.repeat(xlim[0], 9), ys, np.repeat(xlim[1], 9), ys, col="#CCCCCC") circos.rect(np.zeros(9), ys - 0.45, percent, ys + 0.45, col=color, border="white") circos.text( np.repeat(xlim[0], 9), ys, [f"{cat} - {pct}%" for cat, pct in zip(category, percent)], facing="downward", adj=(1.05, 0.5), cex=0.8, ) breaks = np.arange(0, 86, 5) circos.axis(h="top", major_at=breaks, labels=[f"{b}%" for b in breaks], labels_cex=0.6) circos.track(ylim=(0.5, len(percent) + 0.5), track_height=0.8, bg_border=None, panel_fun=panel_bar) circos.clear() A single-sector horizontal circular barplot. When placing labels with circos.text(), setting adj=(1.05, 0.5) right-aligns the text and adds a small proportional horizontal offset from the anchor points. Alternatively, you can use mm_x() to specify the gap in absolute physical units (millimeters). Because physical-to-data conversion along the circular x-axis depends on radial position, pass the bar y-positions via h=ys: circos.text( xlim[0] - mm_x(2.0, h=ys), ys, [f"{cat} - {pct}%" for cat, pct in zip(category, percent)], facing="downward", adj=(1.0, 0.5), cex=0.8, )

title: 5.2 Histograms
text: circlize-py provides circos.trackHist(), a high-level function that computes histograms across sectors, determines a shared y-range, creates a new track, and draws bars via circos.rect(). Setting draw_density=True plots empirical density lines instead of count bars. By default, bin counts and bin widths are calculated independently per sector via Sturges’ rule, which can make bar heights hard to compare across sectors with different sample sizes. Passing a uniform bin_size enforces consistent bin widths across all cells. The example below stacks three tracks: default histogram binning, fixed bin_size=0.1, and draw_density=True. rng = np.random.default_rng(42) x = rng.normal(size=1600) sectors = rng.choice(list("abcdefghijklmnop"), size=1600, replace=True) circos.initialize(sectors, x=x) circos.trackHist(sectors, x=x, col="#999999", border="#999999") circos.trackHist(sectors, x=x, bin_size=0.1, col="#999999", border="#999999") circos.trackHist(sectors, x=x, draw_density=True, col="#999999", border="#999999") circos.clear() Histograms and density lines across three tracks on a circular layout.

title: 5.3 Phylogenetic trees
text: Circular dendrograms are widely used to display phylogenetic trees. In circlize-py, hclust_from_data(), hclust_from_linkage(), and as_dendrogram() produce HClust and DendrogramNode objects compatible with cutree(), color_branches(), and circos.dendrogram(). Here we load the bundled bird.orders phylogenetic dataset with load_extdata("bird.orders"), split it into six clades using cutree(), and color the branches with color_branches(). from circlize import as_dendrogram, circos, color_branches, cutree, load_extdata hc = load_extdata("bird.orders") labels = hc.labels # names of the 23 bird orders ct = cutree(hc, 6) # cut tree into 6 clusters (1..6) n = len(labels) dend = as_dendrogram(hc) Along the circular axis, leaves of a dendrogram sit at 0.5, 1.5, ..., n - 0.5, so initializing a single sector with xlim=(0.0, float(n)) aligns labels and tree tips exactly. On the left panel below, labels are placed in the outer track and the dendrogram faces "outside" (the default) in the inner track: dend = color_branches(dend, k=6, col=list(range(1, 7))) dend_height = float(dend.height) circos.par(cell_padding=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0), points_overflow_warning=False) circos.initialize(["a"], xlim=(0.0, float(n))) circos.track( ylim=(0.0, 1.0), bg_border=None, track_height=0.3, panel_fun=lambda x, y: [ circos.text( i + 0.5, 0.0, labels[i], adj=(0.0, 0.5), facing="clockwise", nice_facing=True, col=ct[labels[i]], cex=0.55, ) for i in range(n) ], ) circos.track( ylim=(0.0, dend_height), bg_border=None, track_height=0.4, panel_fun=lambda x, y: circos.dendrogram(dend), ) circos.clear() Setting facing="inside" flips the dendrogram so its root points outward toward the rim and leaves point inward. In that orientation, add the dendrogram track first and the leaf labels inside it: circos.par(cell_padding=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0), points_overflow_warning=False) circos.initialize(["a"], xlim=(0.0, float(n))) circos.track( ylim=(0.0, dend_height), bg_border=None, track_height=0.4, panel_fun=lambda x, y: circos.dendrogram(dend, facing="inside"), ) circos.track( ylim=(0.0, 1.0), bg_border=None, track_height=0.3, panel_fun=lambda x, y: [ circos.text( i + 0.5, 1.0, labels[i], adj=(1.0, 0.5), facing="clockwise", nice_facing=True, col=ct[labels[i]], cex=0.55, ) for i in range(n) ], ) circos.clear() Circular phylogenetic tree of bird orders with dendrograms facing outside (left) and inside (right).

title: 5.4 Manually create heatmaps
text: Clustered heatmaps can also be assembled manually from circos.rect() and circos.dendrogram(). Below we split a 100 × 10 matrix into two sectors ("a" with 30 rows and "b" with 70 rows) and cluster each subset separately with hclust_from_data(). from circlize import CELL_META, as_dendrogram, circos, color_ramp2, hclust_from_data rng = np.random.default_rng(123) mat = rng.normal(size=(100, 10)) col_fun = color_ramp2([-2.0, 0.0, 2.0], ["green", "black", "red"]) sectors = np.repeat(["a", "b"], [30, 70]) mat_list = { "a": mat[sectors == "a", :], "b": mat[sectors == "b", :], } dend_list = { k: as_dendrogram(hclust_from_data(v)) for k, v in mat_list.items() } In the first track (ylim=(0.0, 10.0)), we reorder rows using dend.leaf_indices() (which returns 0-based row indices in left-to-right dendrogram leaf order) and call circos.rect() vectorized per column. In the second track, we pass max_height equal to the maximum height across both dendrograms so the two trees share a uniform radial scale: circos.par(cell_padding=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0), gap_degree=5) circos.initialize(["a", "b"], xlim=np.array([[0.0, 30.0], [0.0, 70.0]])) def panel_heatmap(x, y): si = CELL_META.sector_index m = mat_list[si] dend = dend_list[si] m2 = m[dend.leaf_indices(), :] col_mat = col_fun(m2) nr, nc = m2.shape xs_left = np.arange(nr, dtype=float) xs_right = xs_left + 1.0 for i in range(nc): circos.rect( xs_left, np.repeat(float(nc - i - 1), nr), xs_right, np.repeat(float(nc - i), nr), border=col_mat[:, i], col=col_mat[:, i], ) circos.track(ylim=(0.0, 10.0), bg_border=None, panel_fun=panel_heatmap) max_height = max(float(d.height) for d in dend_list.values()) circos.track( ylim=(0.0, max_height), bg_border=None, track_height=0.3, panel_fun=lambda x, y: circos.dendrogram( dend_list[CELL_META.sector_index], max_height=max_height, ), ) circos.clear() Manually constructed multi-sector circular heatmaps with aligned dendrograms. In the next chapter, we introduce the high-level circos.heatmap() API, which automates clustering, split tracks, dendrograms, row labels, and inter-row links in just a few calls.

title: 6 The circos.heatmap() function
text: Circular heatmaps are visually striking and compact. In the previous chapter, we built circular heatmaps from low-level circos.rect() and circos.dendrogram() calls. circlize-py provides a high-level circos.heatmap() function that handles row clustering, splitting, dendrograms, row labels, multi-track alignment, and inter-row links automatically. First, we generate a 100 × 10 matrix (df1) with two contrasting sample blocks and randomly assign its rows into five groups ("a" through "e"): import numpy as np import pandas as pd from circlize import circos, color_ramp2 rng = np.random.default_rng(123) mat1 = np.vstack( [ np.hstack([rng.normal(1.0, 1.0, (50, 5)), rng.normal(-1.0, 1.0, (50, 5))]), np.hstack([rng.normal(-1.0, 1.0, (50, 5)), rng.normal(1.0, 1.0, (50, 5))]), ] ) mat1 = mat1[rng.permutation(100), :] df1 = pd.DataFrame( mat1, index=[f"R{i}" for i in range(1, 101)], columns=[f"C{i}" for i in range(1, 11)], ) split = pd.Categorical( rng.choice(list("abcde"), size=100, replace=True), categories=list("abcde"), ordered=True, ) In a standard rectangular heatmap, those five split groups stack vertically: A standard linear split heatmap of df1 split across groups a–e. Next, we turn this layout into circular heatmaps and explore every feature of circos.heatmap().

title: 6.1 Input data
text: circos.heatmap() accepts a 2D NumPy array, a pandas.DataFrame, or a 1D vector/Series (which is automatically reshaped into a single-column matrix). To split rows into separate circular sectors, pass a categorical variable via split (a list/array of strings, or a pd.Categorical / categorical pd.Series; numeric values are converted to strings internally). Colors must be supplied explicitly via col: For continuous numeric data, pass a ColorRamp2 mapping produced by color_ramp2(). For categorical/character data, pass a dict (or pd.Series) mapping category names to colors. In circular heatmaps, matrix rows run along the circular axis and matrix columns run radially: col_fun1 = color_ramp2([-2.0, 0.0, 2.0], ["blue", "white", "red"]) circos.heatmap(df1, split=split, col=col_fun1) circos.clear() A circular heatmap split into five sectors. Important: Always call circos.clear() after finishing a circular heatmap so cached clustering, splitting, and sector metadata are completely reset before the next plot. When split is omitted, the entire matrix is drawn as a single sector: circos.heatmap(df1, col=col_fun1) circos.clear() An unsplit circular heatmap occupying a single sector.

title: 6.2 Circular layout
text: Global layout parameters are controlled via circos.par() prior to calling circos.heatmap(), while track height, borders, and sector labels are passed directly to circos.heatmap(). In the plot below, start_degree=90 begins sector "a" at θ = 90° and progresses clockwise through "e": circos.par(start_degree=90, gap_degree=10, points_overflow_warning=False) circos.heatmap( df1, split=split, col=col_fun1, track_height=0.4, bg_border="green", bg_lwd=2.0, bg_lty=2, show_sector_labels=True, ) circos.clear() Controlling circular layout and sector styling in circos.heatmap(). When split is a pd.Categorical, its categories order determines the clockwise order of sectors; when split is a plain list or array, sectors appear in order of first occurrence (dict.fromkeys). Reversing the category list flips the sector arrangement: # Because circos.clear() reset start_degree to 0, sector "e" begins at θ = 0° split_rev = pd.Categorical( split.astype(str), categories=["e", "d", "c", "b", "a"], ordered=True, ) circos.heatmap(df1, split=split_rev, col=col_fun1, show_sector_labels=True) circos.clear() Controlling sector order with pd.Categorical levels.

title:
6.3 Dendrograms and row
names
text: By default, numeric matrices are clustered on rows. Set dend_side to "inside" or "outside" to draw the row dendrograms in an adjacent track (whose radial thickness is set by dend_track_height): circos.heatmap(df1, split=split, col=col_fun1, dend_side="inside") circos.clear() circos.heatmap(df1, split=split, col=col_fun1, dend_side="outside") circos.clear() Placing row dendrograms inside (left) or outside (right) the heatmap track. When the input DataFrame has non-default row names (index), set rownames_side to "inside" or "outside" to display row labels in their own track: circos.heatmap(df1, split=split, col=col_fun1, rownames_side="inside") circos.clear() circos.heatmap(df1, split=split, col=col_fun1, rownames_side="outside") circos.clear() Placing matrix row names inside (left) or outside (right) the heatmap track. Both dendrograms and row names can be enabled together as long as they sit on opposite sides of the heatmap track: circos.heatmap(df1, split=split, col=col_fun1, dend_side="inside", rownames_side="outside") circos.clear() circos.heatmap(df1, split=split, col=col_fun1, dend_side="outside", rownames_side="inside") circos.clear() Combining dendrograms and row names on opposite sides of the heatmap track. Row-label graphic parameters (rownames_col, rownames_cex, rownames_font) accept either a scalar or a sequence matching the total number of rows in the matrix: nr = len(df1) circos.heatmap( df1, split=split, col=col_fun1, rownames_side="outside", rownames_col=[(i % 10) + 1 for i in range(1, nr + 1)], rownames_cex=rng.uniform(0.3, 2.0, size=nr), rownames_font=[(i % 4) + 1 for i in range(1, nr + 1)], ) circos.clear() Customizing row name colors, sizes, and font faces.

title: 6.4 Clustering
text: Setting cluster=False disables row clustering (no dendrogram is drawn even if dend_side is specified), keeping rows in their original order: circos.heatmap(df1, split=split, col=col_fun1, cluster=True) circos.clear() circos.heatmap(df1, split=split, col=col_fun1, cluster=False) circos.clear() Comparing clustered rows (cluster=True, left) against input row order (cluster=False, right). You can customize the linkage algorithm and distance metric with clustering_method (e.g., "complete", "average", "ward", "single") and distance_method (e.g., "euclidean", "manhattan", "maximum"). Note that circos.heatmap() clusters rows only; to cluster columns as well, reorder columns beforehand using hclust_from_data() and as_dendrogram(): from circlize import as_dendrogram, hclust_from_data col_od = as_dendrogram(hclust_from_data(df1.to_numpy().T)).leaf_indices() circos.heatmap(df1.iloc[:, col_od], split=split, col=col_fun1) circos.clear()

title: 6.5 Callback on dendrograms
text: After each sector’s dendrogram is computed, circos.heatmap() passes it through dend_callback(dend, m, si): dend: the DendrogramNode tree for the current sector. m: the sector’s NumPy sub-matrix. si: the sector name (str). By default, circlize-py reorders branches by row means via reorder_dendrogram(dend, np.nanmean(m, axis=1)). You can substitute any custom DendrogramNode transformer—for instance, a recursive minimum-height node sorter (analogous to dendsort) that places tighter subtrees on the left: from circlize import DendrogramNode def dendsort_node(dend: DendrogramNode) -> DendrogramNode: root = dend.copy() def _sort(node: DendrogramNode) -> float: if node.leaf: return 0.0 scored = [(_sort(c), c) for c in node.children] scored.sort(key=lambda pair: pair[0]) node.children = [p[1] for p in scored] return float(node.height) if all(c.leaf for c in node.children) else min(s for s, _ in scored) _sort(root) root._recompute_stats() return root circos.heatmap( df1, split=split, col=col_fun1, dend_side="inside", dend_callback=lambda dend, m, si: dendsort_node(dend), ) circos.clear() Comparing default row-mean dendrogram ordering (left) with custom minimum-height node sorting (right). Inside dend_callback, color_branches() paints dendrogram branches. Passing k=1 assigns one color per sector, whereas k=4 on an unsplit heatmap highlights four subtrees: from circlize import color_branches dend_col = {s: idx for idx, s in enumerate("abcde", start=1)} circos.heatmap( df1, split=split, col=col_fun1, dend_side="inside", dend_track_height=0.2, dend_callback=lambda dend, m, si: color_branches(dend, k=1, col=[dend_col[si]]), ) circos.clear() Coloring each sector’s dendrogram with a distinct palette color (k=1). circos.heatmap( df1, col=col_fun1, dend_side="inside", dend_track_height=0.2, dend_callback=lambda dend, m, si: color_branches(dend, k=4, col=[2, 3, 4, 5]), ) circos.clear() Coloring four subtrees (k=4) in an unsplit circular heatmap.

title: 6.6 Multiple heatmap tracks
text: The first call to circos.heatmap() initializes the circular layout, splits the rows, and caches each sector’s clustering and row order internally. Subsequent circos.heatmap() calls automatically inherit that exact split and row ordering—which is why calling circos.clear() before starting a new plot is essential. Here df2 is a row-permuted copy of df1. When df1 is drawn first, df1 governs the layout and dendrogram: df2 = df1.iloc[rng.permutation(len(df1)), :].copy() col_fun2 = color_ramp2([-2.0, 0.0, 2.0], ["green", "white", "red"]) circos.heatmap(df1, split=split, col=col_fun1, dend_side="outside") circos.heatmap(df2, col=col_fun2) circos.clear() Two stacked circular heatmap tracks with clustering governed by the first track (df1). Swapping the call order transfers clustering control to df2: circos.heatmap(df2, split=split, col=col_fun2, dend_side="outside") circos.heatmap(df1, col=col_fun1) circos.clear() Swapping track order so df2 governs the shared clustering. When an inner track (or a separate reference matrix) should define the clustering instead of the outermost track, call circos.heatmap.initialize() explicitly first: circos.heatmap.initialize(df1, split=split) circos.heatmap(df2, col=col_fun2, dend_side="outside") circos.heatmap(df1, col=col_fun1) circos.clear() Using circos.heatmap.initialize() so df1 determines clustering even when df2 is the outermost track. Similarly, you can cluster on the full df1 matrix while plotting column subsets across multiple tracks: circos.heatmap.initialize(df1, split=split) circos.heatmap(df1.iloc[:, :5], col=col_fun1) circos.heatmap(df1.iloc[:, 5:], col=col_fun1) circos.clear() Clustering on the full 10-column matrix and displaying two 5-column tracks.

title: 6.7 With other tracks
text: Because heatmap rows occupy [0, 1], [1, 2], ..., [nr - 1, nr] along the circular axis (centered at 0.5, 1.5, ..., nr - 0.5), custom circos.track() panels can align points, lines, or boxplots directly underneath any heatmap track. After circos.heatmap() or circos.heatmap.initialize(), CELL_META exposes three 0-based sector metadata fields in circlize-py: CELL_META.row_dend (or CELL_META.dend): the DendrogramNode for the current sector (None if unclustered). CELL_META.row_order (or CELL_META.order): 0-based row order of the sector’s sub-matrix after clustering (e.g., [8, 11, 0, ...]). CELL_META.subset: sorted 0-based row indices from the original complete matrix belonging to the current sector (e.g., [1, 4, 15, ...]). In sector "a" of our running example, these metadata values look like: CELL_META.row_dend -> DendrogramNode(members=13, height=11.46435) CELL_META.row_order -> [8, 11, 0, 9, 5, 1, 6, 3, 10, 4, 12, 7, 2] CELL_META.subset -> [1, 4, 15, 18, 42, 43, 50, 65, 78, 81, 89, 93, 96] 0-based indexing in circlize-py: Both CELL_META.subset and CELL_META.row_order contain 0-based Python indices, so arr[CELL_META.subset][CELL_META.row_order] aligns any NumPy array directly with the plotted heatmap rows, and x-positions for n rows sit at np.arange(n) + 0.5. Below we plot row means of the first five columns as red/blue points aligned under the heatmap: from circlize import CELL_META mat1_arr = df1.to_numpy() row_mean = mat1_arr[:, :5].mean(axis=1) circos.heatmap(df1, split=split, col=col_fun1) def panel_points(x, y): y_vals = row_mean[CELL_META.subset][CELL_META.row_order] circos.lines(CELL_META.cell_xlim, [0.0, 0.0], lty=2, col="grey") cols = np.where(y_vals > 0.0, "red", "blue") circos.points(np.arange(len(y_vals)) + 0.5, y_vals, col=cols, pch=16, cex=0.5) circos.track( ylim=(float(row_mean.min()), float(row_mean.max())), panel_fun=panel_points, cell_padding=(0.02, 0.0, 0.02, 0.0), ) circos.clear() Adding a row-mean scatter track aligned with a circular heatmap. To place that scatter track outside the heatmap, call circos.heatmap.initialize() first: circos.heatmap.initialize(df1, split=split) circos.track( ylim=(float(row_mean.min()), float(row_mean.max())), panel_fun=panel_points, cell_padding=(0.02, 0.0, 0.02, 0.0), ) circos.heatmap(df1, col=col_fun1) circos.clear() Placing the custom points track outside the heatmap by pre-initializing the heatmap layout. circos.boxplot() summarizes columns of a 2D array, so transposing the reordered 5-column sub-matrix (m.T) draws one boxplot per heatmap row at pos=np.arange(n_rows) + 0.5: circos.heatmap(df1, split=split, col=col_fun1) def panel_boxplot(x, y): m = mat1_arr[CELL_META.subset, :5][CELL_META.row_order, :] n_rows = m.shape[0] circos.boxplot(m.T, pos=np.arange(n_rows) + 0.5, pch=16, cex=0.3) circos.lines(CELL_META.cell_xlim, [0.0, 0.0], lty=2, col="grey") circos.track( ylim=(float(mat1_arr.min()), float(mat1_arr.max())), panel_fun=panel_boxplot, cell_padding=(0.02, 0.0, 0.02, 0.0), ) circos.clear() Aligning per-row boxplots beneath a circular heatmap.

title: 6.8 Add annotations
text: While show_sector_labels=True adds basic sector names, passing track_index=get_current_track_index() to circos.track() lets you decorate the heatmap track with custom curved labels, column names, or column-group bars: from circlize import convert_x, convert_y, get_current_track_index circos.par(points_overflow_warning=False) circos.heatmap(df1, split=split, col=col_fun1) def panel_sector_lbl(x, y): circos.text( CELL_META.xcenter, CELL_META.cell_ylim[1] + float(convert_y(2.0, "mm")), f"this is group {CELL_META.sector_index}", facing="bending.inside", cex=0.8, adj=(0.5, 0.0), nice_facing=True, ) circos.track(track_index=get_current_track_index(), panel_fun=panel_sector_lbl, bg_border=None) circos.clear() Adding custom curved sector labels 2 mm above the heatmap track. To add column names along the radial edge, widen the gap after the last sector (gap_after=[2, 2, 2, 2, 10]) and annotate only when CELL_META.sector_numeric_index == 5 (recall sector_numeric_index is 1-based): circos.par(gap_after=[2, 2, 2, 2, 10], points_overflow_warning=False) circos.heatmap(df1, split=split, col=col_fun1, track_height=0.4) def panel_colnames(x, y): if CELL_META.sector_numeric_index == 5: cn = list(df1.columns) n_cn = len(cn) circos.text( np.repeat(CELL_META.cell_xlim[1], n_cn) + float(convert_x(1.0, "mm")), np.arange(n_cn) + 0.5, cn, cex=0.55, adj=(0.0, 0.5), facing="inside", ) circos.track(track_index=get_current_track_index(), panel_fun=panel_colnames, bg_border=None) circos.clear() Drawing matrix column names inside an expanded gap after the final sector. Using the same gap, circos.rect() and circos.text() can mark groups of columns: circos.par(gap_after=[2, 2, 2, 2, 10], points_overflow_warning=False) circos.heatmap(df1, split=split, col=col_fun1, track_height=0.4) def panel_colgroup(x, y): if CELL_META.sector_numeric_index == 5: x1 = float(CELL_META.cell_xlim[1] + convert_x(1.0, "mm")) x2 = float(CELL_META.cell_xlim[1] + convert_x(5.0, "mm")) xm = float(CELL_META.cell_xlim[1] + convert_x(3.0, "mm")) circos.rect(x1, 0.0, x2, 5.0, col="orange", border=None) circos.text(xm, 2.5, "group 1", cex=0.55, facing="clockwise") circos.rect(x1, 5.0, x2, 10.0, col="pink", border=None) circos.text(xm, 7.5, "group 2", cex=0.55, facing="clockwise") circos.track(track_index=get_current_track_index(), panel_fun=panel_colgroup, bg_border=None) circos.clear() Adding column-group bars and labels inside the sector gap. As explained in the Legends chapter, pair the circular axes with a Matplotlib colorbar via GridSpec: Circular heatmap paired with a Matplotlib colorbar legend.

title:
6.9 A complex example of circular
heatmaps
text: We now convert a multi-omics linear heatmap layout into a multi-track circular visualization with inter-region links and a full set of eight legends. The simulated dataset models 1,000 differentially methylated regions (DMRs) across 20 samples (10 Tumor + 10 Control) alongside their nearest associated genes: mat_meth: 1000 × 20 mean methylation levels (0 to 1). direction: "hyper" or "hypo" methylation change in Tumor vs Control. mat_expr: 1000 × 20 row-standardized (z-scored) gene expression negatively correlated with methylation. cor_pvalue: -log10(p-value) for the Pearson correlation between methylation and expression. gene_type: "protein_coding", "lincRNA", "microRNA", "psedo-gene", or "others". anno_gene: gene model annotation ("intragenic", "TSS", or "intergenic"). dist: genomic distance from each DMR to its target gene TSS. anno_enhancer: 1000 × 3 enhancer overlap fractions (0 to 1). Rows are partitioned into five clusters (cluster1–cluster5) by k-means (scipy.cluster.vq.kmeans2) on mat_meth: Linear multi-track reference view of the 1,000-DMR multi-omics dataset. Using circos.heatmap(), all eight data tracks stack from outside (mat_meth) to inside (anno_enhancer), sharing the clustering and sector split defined by mat_meth: from circlize import color_ramp2, rand_color col_meth = color_ramp2([0.0, 0.5, 1.0], ["blue", "white", "red"]) col_direction = {"hyper": "red", "hypo": "blue"} col_expr = color_ramp2([-2.0, 0.0, 2.0], ["green", "white", "red"]) col_pvalue = color_ramp2([0.0, 2.0, 4.0], ["white", "white", "red"]) col_gene_type = dict( zip( ["protein_coding", "lincRNA", "microRNA", "psedo-gene", "others"], ["#8DD3C7", "#FFFFB3", "#BEBADA", "#FB8072", "#80B1D3"], ) ) col_anno_gene = dict(zip(["intragenic", "TSS", "intergenic"], ["#E41A1C", "#377EB8", "#4DAF4A"])) col_dist = color_ramp2([0.0, 10000.0], ["black", "white"]) col_enhancer = color_ramp2([0.0, 1.0], ["white", "orange"]) circos.heatmap(mat_meth, split=km, col=col_meth, track_height=0.12) circos.heatmap(direction, col=col_direction, track_height=0.01) circos.heatmap(mat_expr, col=col_expr, track_height=0.12) circos.heatmap(cor_pvalue, col=col_pvalue, track_height=0.01) circos.heatmap(gene_type, col=col_gene_type, track_height=0.01) circos.heatmap(anno_gene, col=col_anno_gene, track_height=0.01) circos.heatmap(dist, col=col_dist, track_height=0.01) circos.heatmap(anno_enhancer, col=col_enhancer, track_height=0.03) circos.clear() Eight-track circular multi-omics heatmap of methylation, expression, correlation, gene annotations, TSS distance, and enhancer overlap. Suppose we have 20 pairwise 3D chromatin interactions between DMRs stored in df_link with 0-based row indices from_index and to_index. Manually resolving each DMR’s circular position requires finding its sector (km[idx]), fetching that sector’s subset and row_order metadata, locating the row’s 0-based position in [sub[i] for i in row_order], and adding 0.5: from circlize import get_cell_meta_data for from_idx, to_idx in zip(df_link["from_index"], df_link["to_index"]): g1 = str(km[from_idx]) g2 = str(km[to_idx]) sub1 = get_cell_meta_data("subset", sector_index=g1) ord1 = get_cell_meta_data("row_order", sector_index=g1) x1 = [sub1[k] for k in ord1].index(from_idx) + 0.5 sub2 = get_cell_meta_data("subset", sector_index=g2) ord2 = get_cell_meta_data("row_order", sector_index=g2) x2 = [sub2[k] for k in ord2].index(to_idx) + 0.5 circos.link(g1, x1, g2, x2, col=rand_color(1)[0]) circos.heatmap.link() encapsulates that exact lookup and accepts either 0-based integer row indices or row-name strings (when the first matrix passed to circos.heatmap() is a DataFrame with string index labels): for from_idx, to_idx in zip(df_link["from_index"], df_link["to_index"]): circos.heatmap.link(int(from_idx), int(to_idx), col=rand_color(1)[0]) # Or link directly by DataFrame row names: circos.heatmap.link("DMR10", "DMR420", col="#D95F02", lwd=1.6) Adding 20 inter-DMR links inside the eight-track multi-omics circular heatmap.
