title:
14 The chordDiagram()
function
text: One unique feature of circular layouts is visualizing relations between objects with links, as illustrated in tabular visualization examples at circos.ca. This style of graphic is known as a Chord diagram. In circlize-py, chord_diagram() (also available via the R-style alias chordDiagram()) makes it straightforward to draw Chord diagrams either with minimal defaults or with fine-grained customization. Relations can be represented in two data formats: an adjacency matrix or an adjacency list. In an adjacency matrix, the entry in the i-th row and j-th column gives the connection from row object i to column object j, with the absolute value measuring connection strength. In an adjacency list, relations are stored as a three-column pandas.DataFrame where links go from the first column to the second column with strength in the third column. An adjacency matrix can be represented as a labeled pandas.DataFrame (or a 2D numpy.ndarray): import numpy as np import pandas as pd mat = pd.DataFrame( np.arange(1, 10).reshape((3, 3), order="F"), index=list("abc"), columns=list("ABC"), ) mat A B C a 1 4 7 b 2 5 8 c 3 6 9 An adjacency list is a DataFrame with source, target, and value columns: df = pd.DataFrame({"from": list("abc"), "to": list("ABC"), "value": [1, 2, 3]}) df from to value 0 a A 1 1 b B 2 2 c C 3 You can convert cleanly between these two formats using circlize_py.adjacency_matrix2list() and circlize_py.adjacency_list2matrix(). A Chord diagram communicates relational structure at several levels: Links directly connect pairs of related objects. Link widths are proportional to relation strength, making magnitude comparisons immediate. Link colors provide an additional visual encoding (e.g., source identity, sign, or continuous intensity). Sector widths show each object’s total connection strength across all incoming and outgoing links. In circlize-py, chord_diagram() accepts both adjacency matrices (np.ndarray or named pd.DataFrame) and adjacency lists (pd.DataFrame), returning a pd.DataFrame with link coordinates (['rn', 'cn', 'value1', 'value2', 'o1', 'o2', 'x1', 'x2'], plus 'col' when plotted). Depending on the input format, per-link graphical parameters take either a 2D array / matrix-shaped DataFrame / 3-column lookup DataFrame (for matrix input) or a 1D vector/Series matching the number of rows (for adjacency-list input). Below we focus primarily on matrix examples while showing the corresponding adjacency-list idioms alongside them.

title:
14.1 Basic usage of making Chord
diagram
text: First, let’s build a random 3x6 adjacency matrix and its equivalent adjacency list: import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd from circlize_py import chord_diagram, circos, color_ramp2, mm_h, rand_color rng = np.random.default_rng(999) arr = rng.permutation(np.arange(1, 19)).reshape((3, 6), order="F") rn = [f"S{i}" for i in range(1, 4)] cn = [f"E{i}" for i in range(1, 7)] mat = pd.DataFrame(arr, index=rn, columns=cn) df = pd.DataFrame( { "from": np.tile(rn, len(cn)), "to": np.repeat(cn, len(rn)), "value": arr.ravel(order="F"), } ) The simplest plot just calls chord_diagram(mat) (followed by circos.clear() to reset layout state): chord_diagram(mat) circos.clear() Basic usages of chord_diagram(). Calling chord_diagram(df) with the adjacency list produces the same diagram: chord_diagram(df) circos.clear() By default, a Chord diagram contains a sector-label track, a grid track with axes, and connecting ribbons. Row sectors appear in the lower half of the circle and column sectors in the upper half, ordered by union(mat.index, mat.columns) (or union(df.iloc[:, 0], df.iloc[:, 1])). You can reorder sectors with order, whose length must match the total number of sectors. Keeping row sectors (S*) contiguous and column sectors (E*) contiguous improves readability; interleaving them creates unnecessary crossings. See Multiple-group Chord diagram for grouping more than two sets. fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.6, 4.3)) plt.sca(ax1) chord_diagram(mat, order=["S2", "S1", "S3", "E4", "E1", "E5", "E2", "E6", "E3"]) circos.clear() plt.sca(ax2) chord_diagram(mat, order=["S2", "S1", "E4", "E1", "S3", "E5", "E2", "E6", "E3"]) circos.clear() Adjust sector orders in Chord diagram. Left: sectors remain grouped after reordering; right: sectors are interleaved. By default, grid colors are randomly assigned and each link inherits its row sector’s color with transparency=0.5.

title: 14.2 Adjust by circos.par()
text: Because chord_diagram() is built on top of standard circlize_py tracks, global layout parameters in circos.par() apply directly. Remember to call circos.clear() afterward so customized circos.par() values do not leak into subsequent plots. You can set sector gaps explicitly via circos.par(gap_after=...) (an alias for gap_degree) to visually separate row sectors from column sectors: circos.par(gap_after=[5] * (mat.shape[0] - 1) + [15] + [5] * (mat.shape[1] - 1) + [15]) chord_diagram(mat) circos.clear() Set gaps in Chord diagram via circos.par(gap_after=...). With an adjacency list: circos.par( gap_after=[5] * (df["from"].nunique() - 1) + [15] + [5] * (df["to"].nunique() - 1) + [15] ) chord_diagram(df) circos.clear() As explained in Graphic parameters, gap_after can also be a dictionary mapping sector names to gap angles: circos.par( gap_after={ "S1": 5, "S2": 5, "S3": 15, "E1": 5, "E2": 5, "E3": 5, "E4": 5, "E5": 5, "E6": 15, } ) chord_diagram(mat) circos.clear() For the common two-group case where row and column names do not overlap, passing big_gap directly to chord_diagram() sets the gap between the two groups automatically, while small_gap (default 1.0) controls the spacing within each group: chord_diagram(mat, big_gap=30) circos.clear() Directly set big_gap in chord_diagram(). The first sector begins at circos.par(start_degree=...) (default 0, right center) and proceeds clockwise when clock_wise=True. Setting clock_wise=False reverses direction, which twists links unless sector order is also adjusted; reversing order while keeping clock_wise=True preserves clean link routing: fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.6, 4.3)) plt.sca(ax1) circos.par(start_degree=85, clock_wise=False) chord_diagram(mat) circos.clear() plt.sca(ax2) circos.par(start_degree=85) chord_diagram(mat, order=list(reversed(mat.columns)) + list(reversed(mat.index))) circos.clear() Change start position and orientation of Chord diagram. Left: clock_wise=False; right: reversed order with default clockwise routing.

title: 14.3.1 Set grid colors
text: By default, links take the color of their source (row / first-column) sector. grid_col sets sector grid colors, ideally via a dictionary keyed by sector name (or a sequence matching sector order). To color links by column sectors instead of row sectors, transpose the matrix (mat.T): grid_col = { "S1": "red", "S2": "green", "S3": "blue", "E1": "grey", "E2": "grey", "E3": "grey", "E4": "grey", "E5": "grey", "E6": "grey", } fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.6, 4.3)) plt.sca(ax1) chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col) circos.clear() plt.sca(ax2) chord_diagram(mat.T, grid_col=grid_col) circos.clear() Set grid colors in Chord diagram. Left: mat; right: mat.T colors links by E* sectors.

title: 14.3.2 Set link colors
text: transparency controls link opacity from 0 (completely opaque) to 1 (completely transparent), defaulting to 0.5: chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, transparency=0) circos.clear() Opaque links (transparency=0) in Chord diagram. For matrix input, you can supply a 2D array (or DataFrame) of link colors matching mat.shape. When explicit alpha values are already encoded in the colors (e.g., via rand_color(..., transparency=0.5)), transparency is preserved: col_mat = np.asarray(rand_color(mat.size, transparency=0.5), dtype=object).reshape(mat.shape, order="F") chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, col=col_mat) circos.clear() Set a 2D color matrix for links in Chord diagram. For an adjacency list df, pass a 1D list or Series of length len(df): col = rand_color(len(df)) chord_diagram(df, grid_col=grid_col, col=col) circos.clear() When relation values are continuous, col accepts a color_ramp2() mapping function: col_fun = color_ramp2( [float(mat.to_numpy().min()), float(mat.to_numpy().max())], ["#FFEEEE", "#FF0000"], transparency=0.5, ) chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, col=col_fun) circos.clear() Set a color_ramp2() color mapping function for links. The same callable works with adjacency lists: chord_diagram(df, grid_col=grid_col, col=col_fun) # or equivalently: chord_diagram(df, grid_col=grid_col, col=col_fun(df["value"])) circos.clear() For matrix input, row_col and column_col let you color links by row or column without affecting grid colors (R integer palette indices 1..8, named colors, and hex strings are all accepted): fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.6, 4.3)) plt.sca(ax1) chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, row_col=[1, 2, 3]) circos.clear() plt.sca(ax2) chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, column_col=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]) circos.clear() Color links by row (row_col) or column (column_col) independently of grid_col. As before, any alpha channel already included in col, row_col, or column_col overrides the global transparency argument. See Highlight links for selective highlighting.

title: 14.4 Link border
text: link_lwd, link_lty, and link_border control ribbon border width, line style, and border color. Each accepts a scalar, a 2D array matching mat.shape, or a 3-column DataFrame. With scalar values, all links share the same border style: chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, link_lwd=2, link_lty=2, link_border="red") circos.clear() Uniform scalar link border style in Chord diagram. With full matrices matching mat.shape, use np.nan (or "none") for links that should have no visible border: lwd_mat = np.ones(mat.shape, dtype=float) lwd_mat[mat.to_numpy() > 12] = 2.0 border_mat = np.full(mat.shape, np.nan, dtype=object) border_mat[mat.to_numpy() > 12] = "red" chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, link_lwd=lwd_mat, link_border=border_mat) circos.clear() Set link line width and border color as matrices. To style a single row or subset of links while keeping other links borderless, fill a matrix with np.nan and assign colors to the target slice (or use a 3-column DataFrame when all links have explicit styles): border_mat2 = np.full(mat.shape, np.nan, dtype=object) border_mat2[1, :] = "black" # highlight row S2 chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, link_lwd=2, link_border=border_mat2) circos.clear() Highlight borders for a single row (S2) in the matrix. You can also pass a three-column DataFrame (row_name, col_name, value) for link_lty, link_lwd, and link_border: lty_df = pd.DataFrame({"rn": ["S1", "S2", "S3"], "cn": ["E5", "E6", "E4"], "lty": [1, 2, 3]}) lwd_df = pd.DataFrame({"rn": ["S1", "S2", "S3"], "cn": ["E5", "E6", "E4"], "lwd": [2, 2, 2]}) border_df = pd.DataFrame({"rn": ["S1", "S2", "S3"], "cn": ["E5", "E6", "E4"], "border": [1, 1, 1]}) chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, link_lty=lty_df, link_lwd=lwd_df, link_border=border_df) circos.clear() Set link line style, width, and border via three-column DataFrames. For an adjacency list df, pass vectors matching len(df): rng_s = np.random.default_rng(1) chord_diagram( df, grid_col=grid_col, link_lty=rng_s.integers(1, 4, size=len(df)), link_lwd=rng_s.uniform(0.5, 2.0, size=len(df)), link_border=rng_s.integers(0, 2, size=len(df)), ) circos.clear()

title: 14.5 Highlight links
text: Beyond link borders, you can highlight key relations by adjusting link colors and transparency or by filtering visibility. To emphasize all links originating from one sector (S1), pass per-row colors with low alpha for the remaining rows: chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, row_col=["#FF000080", "#00FF0010", "#0000FF10"]) circos.clear() Highlight links from S1 by varying transparency across rows. To highlight links above a numeric threshold, set smaller entries in a color matrix to "#00000000" (fully transparent): col_mat_hl = col_mat.copy() col_mat_hl[mat.to_numpy() < 12] = "#00000000" chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, col=col_mat_hl) circos.clear() Highlight strong links (value >= 12) using a color matrix. Equivalently, use a threshold function for either matrix or adjacency-list input: col_fun_hl = lambda x: np.where(np.asarray(x) < 12, "#00000000", "#FF000080") chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, col=col_fun_hl) circos.clear() While transparent links are still drawn (preserving sector widths), passing a three-column DataFrame to col draws only the listed links while still sizing sectors from the full matrix: col_df = pd.DataFrame( { "rn": ["S1", "S2", "S3"], "cn": ["E5", "E6", "E4"], "col": ["#FF000080", "#00FF0080", "#0000FF80"], } ) chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, col=col_df) circos.clear() Draw only highlighted links using a three-column color DataFrame. For an adjacency list, you can also modify a color vector directly: col = np.asarray(rand_color(len(df)), dtype=object) col[df["value"].to_numpy() < 10] = "#00000000" chord_diagram(df, grid_col=grid_col, col=col) circos.clear() When transparency is undesirable or you want links omitted completely from rendering without changing sector sizes, use link_visible with a boolean matrix or boolean vector: chord_diagram(df, grid_col=grid_col, link_visible=df["value"] >= 10) circos.clear() Filter rendered links using link_visible.

title: 14.6 Orders of links
text: By default, chord_diagram() arranges link endpoints within each sector to minimize crossings. To sort links on each sector by width instead, set link_sort=True and control direction with link_decreasing: fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.6, 4.5)) plt.sca(ax1) chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, link_sort=True, link_decreasing=True) ax1.set_title("link_sort = True, link_decreasing = True", fontsize=9.5) circos.clear() plt.sca(ax2) chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, link_sort=True, link_decreasing=False) ax2.set_title("link_sort = True, link_decreasing = False", fontsize=9.5) circos.clear() Sort link widths within sectors using link_sort and link_decreasing.

title: 14.7 z-index of adding links
text: Links are normally drawn in matrix/DataFrame row order. When drawing opaque links (transparency=0), wide ribbons drawn early may be covered by narrower ones drawn later. Setting link_zindex places links with larger z-index values on top: from scipy.stats import rankdata zmat = rankdata(mat.to_numpy()).reshape(mat.shape) fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.6, 4.5)) plt.sca(ax1) chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, transparency=0) ax1.set_title("Default z-order", fontsize=10) circos.clear() plt.sca(ax2) chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, transparency=0, link_zindex=zmat) ax2.set_title("link_zindex = rank(mat)", fontsize=10) circos.clear() Control link layering with link_zindex. For an adjacency list: chord_diagram(df, grid_col=grid_col, transparency=0, link_zindex=rankdata(df["value"])) circos.clear() As a convenient shortcut for placing wider ribbons above narrower ones without computing ranks manually, set link_largest_ontop=True: fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.6, 4.5)) plt.sca(ax1) chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, transparency=0, link_largest_ontop=False) ax1.set_title("link_largest_ontop = False", fontsize=10) circos.clear() plt.sca(ax2) chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, transparency=0, link_largest_ontop=True) ax2.set_title("link_largest_ontop = True", fontsize=10) circos.clear() Place largest links on top using link_largest_ontop=True.

title: 14.8 Self-links
text: When an entry connects a sector to itself, self_link controls whether the self-link consumes one interval (self_link=1) or two intervals (self_link=2, duplicating the width in sector totals): df2 = pd.DataFrame({"start": ["a", "b", "c", "a"], "end": ["a", "a", "b", "c"]}) fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.6, 4.5)) plt.sca(ax1) chord_diagram(df2, grid_col=[1, 2, 3], self_link=1) ax1.set_title("self_link = 1", fontsize=10) circos.clear() plt.sca(ax2) chord_diagram(df2, grid_col=[1, 2, 3], self_link=2) ax2.set_title("self_link = 2", fontsize=10) circos.clear() Comparison of self_link=1 and self_link=2 on sector a.

title: 14.9 Symmetric matrix
text: For symmetric matrices (such as correlation matrices), setting symmetric=True plots only the lower triangular entries without the diagonal, avoiding duplicate links: rng_sym = np.random.default_rng(42) mat3 = rng_sym.normal(size=(5, 5)) cor_mat = pd.DataFrame(np.corrcoef(mat3, rowvar=False), index=list("abcde"), columns=list("abcde")) col_fun_sym = color_ramp2([-1, 0, 1], ["green", "white", "red"]) fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.6, 4.5)) plt.sca(ax1) chord_diagram(cor_mat, grid_col=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5], symmetric=True, col=col_fun_sym) ax1.set_title("symmetric = True", fontsize=10) circos.clear() plt.sca(ax2) chord_diagram(cor_mat, grid_col=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5], col=col_fun_sym) ax2.set_title("symmetric = False", fontsize=10) circos.clear() Symmetric matrix handling (symmetric=True vs symmetric=False).

title: 14.10 Directional relations
text: When rows and columns (or the first and second DataFrame columns) have a meaningful direction, set directional=1 (from rows to columns), directional=-1 (from columns to rows), or directional=2 (bi-directional). By default, direction_type="diffHeight" shortens the starting end by diff_height (mm_h(2) by default; use a negative diff_height to make the source end taller instead): fig, (ax1, ax2, ax3) = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.5, 3.6)) plt.sca(ax1) chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, directional=1) circos.clear() plt.sca(ax2) chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, directional=1, diff_height=mm_h(5)) circos.clear() plt.sca(ax3) chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, directional=-1) circos.clear() Represent link directions with unequal endpoint radii (diff_height). Directional mode is especially helpful when row names and column names overlap: rng2 = np.random.default_rng(77) mat2 = pd.DataFrame( rng2.permutation(np.arange(1, 101))[:35].reshape((5, 7), order="F"), index=list("abcde"), columns=list("abcdefg"), ) chord_diagram(mat2, grid_col=list(range(1, 8)), directional=1, row_col=list(range(1, 6))) circos.clear() Directional Chord diagram where row and column sector names overlap. To suppress self-loops in such a matrix, zero out the shared diagonal entries before plotting: mat3_ns = mat2.copy() for cn_name in set(mat3_ns.index) & set(mat3_ns.columns): mat3_ns.loc[cn_name, cn_name] = 0 chord_diagram(mat3_ns, grid_col=list(range(1, 8)), directional=1, row_col=list(range(1, 6))) circos.clear() Directional Chord diagram with self-links removed. Links can also display center arrows by setting direction_type="arrows" (or ["diffHeight", "arrows"]). In circlize-py, you can apply arrows selectively to a subset of links by passing a matrix or three-column DataFrame to direction_type: dt_mat = np.full(mat.shape, "none", dtype=object) dt_mat[0, 4] = "arrows" # S1 -> E5 dt_mat[1, 5] = "arrows" # S2 -> E6 dt_mat[2, 3] = "arrows" # S3 -> E4 chord_diagram( mat, grid_col=grid_col, directional=1, direction_type=dt_mat, link_arr_col="black", link_arr_length=0.2, ) circos.clear() Center arrows added to a subset of directional links. Combining "diffHeight" and "arrows" gives a clear indication at both the link ends and center: dt_df = pd.DataFrame( { "rn": ["S1", "S2", "S3"], "cn": ["E5", "E6", "E4"], "type": ["diffHeight+arrows", "diffHeight+arrows", "diffHeight+arrows"], } ) chord_diagram( mat, grid_col=grid_col, directional=1, direction_type=dt_df, link_arr_col="black", link_arr_length=0.2, ) circos.clear() Combine diffHeight and center arrows on selected links. When there are many links, link_arr_type="big.arrow" shapes the ribbon tip itself into an arrowhead instead of drawing separate center arrows: rng_x = np.random.default_rng(123) matx = rng_x.normal(size=(8, 8)) chord_diagram( matx, directional=1, direction_type=["diffHeight", "arrows"], link_arr_type="big.arrow", ) circos.clear() Use link_arr_type="big.arrow" for dense directional matrices. Setting diff_height negative swaps which end is longer: chord_diagram( matx, directional=1, direction_type=["diffHeight", "arrows"], link_arr_type="big.arrow", diff_height=-mm_h(2), ) circos.clear() big.arrow with negative diff_height=-mm_h(2). The same directional options work directly on adjacency-list DataFrames (chord_diagram(df, directional=1)). When directional=1 and diff_height > 0, colored indicator bars along the inner edge of source sectors show the proportion going to each target sector. Disable them with link_target_prop=False or resize them with target_prop_height: fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.6, 4.3)) plt.sca(ax1) chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, directional=1, link_target_prop=False) circos.clear() plt.sca(ax2) chord_diagram( mat, grid_col=grid_col, directional=1, diff_height=mm_h(10), target_prop_height=mm_h(8), ) circos.clear() Control target-proportion indicator bars with link_target_prop and target_prop_height.

title: 14.11 Scaling
text: By default, sector widths reflect absolute sums of relation values. Setting scale=True scales every sector to [0, 1] so link widths show relative fractions within each sector: fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.6, 4.5)) plt.sca(ax1) chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col) ax1.set_title("Default", fontsize=10) circos.clear() plt.sca(ax2) chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, scale=True) ax2.set_title("scale = True", fontsize=10) circos.clear() Scaling each sector from 0 to 1 (scale=True).

title: 14.12 Reduce
text: Sectors whose total contribution falls below reduce (default 1e-5, as a fraction of the total sum across all sectors) are automatically dropped along with their links and color/gap entries: mat_red = pd.DataFrame( np.random.default_rng(123).normal(size=(6, 6)), index=[f"R{i}" for i in range(1, 7)], columns=[f"C{i}" for i in range(1, 7)], ) mat_red.iloc[1, :] = 1e-10 mat_red.iloc[:, 2] = 1e-10 chord_diagram(mat_red) circos.info() circos.clear() All your sectors: ['R1', 'R3', 'R4', 'R5', 'R6', 'C1', 'C2', 'C4', 'C5', 'C6'] All your tracks: [1, 2] Both R2 and C3 were removed automatically. You can also set rows or columns explicitly to 0 to achieve the same effect.

title: 14.13 Input as a data frame
text: When the input is an adjacency-list DataFrame, each row corresponds to a single link, and per-link parameters (transparency, col, link_border, link_lwd, link_lty, link_arr_length, link_arr_width, link_arr_type, link_arr_lwd, link_arr_lty, link_arr_col, link_visible, link_zindex) can be supplied as 1D sequences matching len(df). Beyond parity with matrices, DataFrames support two unique capabilities and sub-interval overlapping layouts.

title:
14.13.1 Multiple links between two
sectors
text: Unlike an adjacency matrix, a DataFrame can contain multiple rows for the same sector pair—for example, separate positive and negative links: rng_m = np.random.default_rng(55) pairs = [(r, c) for c in list("ABCD") for r in list("abc")] df_pos = pd.DataFrame(pairs, columns=["from", "to"]) df_pos["value"] = rng_m.integers(1, 11, size=len(pairs)) df_neg = pd.DataFrame(pairs, columns=["from", "to"]) df_neg["value"] = -rng_m.integers(1, 11, size=len(pairs)) df_multi = pd.concat([df_pos, df_neg], ignore_index=True) grid_col_m = {s: idx for idx, s in enumerate(list("abcABCD"), start=1)} chord_diagram( df_multi, col=np.where(df_multi["value"] > 0, "red", "green"), grid_col=grid_col_m, ) circos.clear() Multiple links (positive in red, negative in green) between the same sector pairs. Using link_visible, you can split positive and negative links across two side-by-side diagrams while keeping identical sector widths: fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.6, 4.5)) plt.sca(ax1) chord_diagram(df_multi, col="red", link_visible=df_multi["value"] > 0, grid_col=grid_col_m) ax1.set_title("Positive links", fontsize=10) circos.clear() plt.sca(ax2) chord_diagram(df_multi, col="green", link_visible=df_multi["value"] < 0, grid_col=grid_col_m) ax2.set_title("Negative links", fontsize=10) circos.clear() Split positive and negative links while preserving sector sizes.

title:
14.13.2 Unequal width of the link
ends
text: If a DataFrame contains two numeric columns (columns 3 and 4), the first specifies the link width at the source sector (rn) and the second specifies the width at the target sector (cn): df_uneq = pd.DataFrame(pairs, columns=["from", "to"]) df_uneq["value"] = 1 df_uneq["value2"] = 3 fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.6, 4.5)) plt.sca(ax1) chord_diagram(df_uneq.iloc[:, :3], grid_col=grid_col_m) ax1.set_title("One column of values", fontsize=10) circos.clear() plt.sca(ax2) chord_diagram(df_uneq.iloc[:, :4], grid_col=grid_col_m) ax2.set_title("Two columns of values", fontsize=10) circos.clear() Equal vs. unequal link endpoint widths from one vs. two numeric DataFrame columns.

title:
14.13.3 Overlapping
incoming and outgoing link intervals (link_overlap)
text: When row and column sector names overlap in a directional diagram (directional=1 or -1), incoming and outgoing links are placed side-by-side along each sector by default (link_overlap=False). Setting link_overlap=True overlays outgoing (x1) and incoming (x2) sub-intervals on the same [0, max(out, in)] sector span: mat_ov = pd.DataFrame( [[0, 12, 8, 5], [6, 0, 10, 4], [9, 7, 0, 11], [3, 14, 6, 0]], index=list("abcd"), columns=list("abcd"), ) gcol_ov = {"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3, "d": 4} fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.6, 4.5)) plt.sca(ax1) chord_diagram(mat_ov, grid_col=gcol_ov, directional=1, link_overlap=False) ax1.set_title("link_overlap = False", fontsize=10) circos.clear() plt.sca(ax2) chord_diagram(mat_ov, grid_col=gcol_ov, directional=1, link_overlap=True) ax2.set_title("link_overlap = True", fontsize=10) circos.clear() Comparing side-by-side (link_overlap=False) and overlaid (link_overlap=True) sub-intervals.

title:
15 Advanced usage of
chordDiagram()
text: The default style of chord_diagram() (or chordDiagram()) handles most relational plots cleanly, and because it is built on standard circlize-py tracks, you can customize track layouts, sector labels, axes, symmetry, cross-diagram scales, and multi-group arrangements in depth. Since matrix and adjacency-list inputs share the same customization pipeline, we illustrate these techniques with adjacency matrices (pandas.DataFrame / numpy.ndarray). Throughout this chapter, we reuse the 3x6 example matrix mat and color dictionary grid_col: import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd from circlize_py import ( CELL_META, calc_gap, chord_diagram, circos, ensure_canvas, get_all_sector_index, get_cell_meta_data, highlight, mm_h, strwidth_canvas, ) rng = np.random.default_rng(999) arr = rng.permutation(np.arange(1, 19)).reshape((3, 6), order="F") mat = pd.DataFrame(arr, index=[f"S{i}" for i in range(1, 4)], columns=[f"E{i}" for i in range(1, 7)]) grid_col = { "S1": "red", "S2": "green", "S3": "blue", "E1": "grey", "E2": "grey", "E3": "grey", "E4": "grey", "E5": "grey", "E6": "grey", }

title: 15.1 Organization of tracks
text: By default, chord_diagram() creates two tracks: track 1 for sector names and track 2 for colored grids with axes: chord_diagram(mat) circos.info() circos.clear() All your sectors: ['S1', 'S2', 'S3', 'E1', 'E2', 'E3', 'E4', 'E5', 'E6'] All your tracks: [1, 2] Your current sector.index is E6 Your current track.index is 2 These tracks are controlled via annotation_track (any subset of ["name", "grid", "axis"], or None) and annotation_track_height (relative to the unit circle radius, or physical units via mm_h()). Axes are drawn only when "grid" is included in annotation_track: fig, (ax1, ax2, ax3) = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.5, 3.6)) plt.sca(ax1) chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, annotation_track="grid") circos.clear() plt.sca(ax2) chord_diagram( mat, grid_col=grid_col, annotation_track=["name", "grid"], annotation_track_height=[0.03, 0.01], ) circos.clear() plt.sca(ax3) chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, annotation_track=None) circos.clear() Track organization controlled by annotation_track and annotation_track_height. You can pre-allocate empty outer tracks before drawing the Chord diagram using pre_allocate_tracks, then populate them later: chord_diagram(mat, pre_allocate_tracks=2) circos.info() circos.clear() All your sectors: ['S1', 'S2', 'S3', 'E1', 'E2', 'E3', 'E4', 'E5', 'E6'] All your tracks: [1, 2, 3, 4] Your current sector.index is E6 Your current track.index is 4 Each pre-allocated track uses the following defaults, which can be overridden by passing a dict (single track) or a list[dict] (multiple tracks): { "ylim": [0.0, 1.0], "track_height": circos.par("track.height"), "bg_col": None, "bg_border": None, "bg_lty": 1, "bg_lwd": 1.0, "track_margin": circos.par("track.margin"), } For example: chord_diagram(mat, annotation_track=None, pre_allocate_tracks={"track_height": 0.3}) circos.clear() # Or two pre-allocated tracks with per-track dictionaries: chord_diagram( mat, annotation_track=None, pre_allocate_tracks=[{"track_height": 0.1}, {"bg_border": "black"}], ) circos.clear()

title: 15.2 Customize sector labels
text: Because chord_diagram() does not directly expose text-facing options for sector labels, the cleanest approach is to omit "name" from annotation_track, pre-allocate an outer track, and populate track 1 afterward with circos.track(track_index=1, ..., bg_border=None). Remember to pass bg_border=None so track 1 stays borderless: ax = ensure_canvas(initialize=True) max_w = max(strwidth_canvas(s, ax=ax) for s in list(mat.index) + list(mat.columns)) chord_diagram( mat, grid_col=grid_col, annotation_track="grid", pre_allocate_tracks={"track_height": max_w}, ) circos.track( track_index=1, bg_border=None, panel_fun=lambda x, y: circos.text( CELL_META.xcenter, CELL_META.ylim[0], CELL_META.sector_index, facing="clockwise", nice_facing=True, adj=(0.0, 0.5), ), ) circos.clear() Clockwise radial sector labels added in a pre-allocated outer track. When labels are long and oriented radially ("clockwise" or "reverse.clockwise"), they can extend past the unit circle. Measuring the longest label with strwidth_canvas() and dynamically expanding circos.par(circle_margin=...) (or canvas_xlim / canvas_ylim) keeps every label comfortably inside the figure: mat_long = mat.copy() mat_long.index = [f"Source_Group_{i}" for i in range(1, 4)] mat_long.columns = [f"Endpoint_Category_{i}" for i in range(1, 7)] gcol_long = { **{f"Source_Group_{i}": c for i, c in enumerate(["red", "green", "blue"], 1)}, **{f"Endpoint_Category_{i}": "grey" for i in range(1, 7)}, } ax = ensure_canvas(initialize=True) max_long_w = max( strwidth_canvas(s, cex=0.8, ax=ax) for s in list(mat_long.index) + list(mat_long.columns) ) margin = max(0.05, max_long_w * 1.15) circos.par(circle_margin=(margin, margin, margin, margin)) chord_diagram( mat_long, grid_col=gcol_long, annotation_track="grid", pre_allocate_tracks={"track_height": 0.05}, ) circos.par(points_overflow_warning=False) circos.track( track_index=1, bg_border=None, panel_fun=lambda x, y: circos.text( CELL_META.xcenter, CELL_META.ylim[0], CELL_META.sector_index, facing="clockwise", nice_facing=True, adj=(0.0, 0.5), cex=0.8, ), ) circos.clear() Long rotated clockwise sector labels accommodated via dynamic circle_margin. You can also place sector names directly inside the grid bars by explicitly passing sector_index and track_index to get_cell_meta_data() and circos.text(): chord_diagram( mat, grid_col=grid_col, annotation_track=["grid", "axis"], annotation_track_height=mm_h(5), ) for si in get_all_sector_index(): xlim = get_cell_meta_data("xlim", sector_index=si, track_index=1) ylim = get_cell_meta_data("ylim", sector_index=si, track_index=1) circos.text( float(np.mean(xlim)), float(np.mean(ylim)), si, sector_index=si, track_index=1, facing="bending.inside", nice_facing=True, col="white", ) circos.clear() Curved sector labels drawn inside the grid cells. Or choose label orientation dynamically based on each sector’s angular width (abs(xplot[1] - xplot[0])): narrow sectors get radial "clockwise" labels while wide sectors get tangential "inside" labels: rng2 = np.random.default_rng(123) mat2 = np.abs(rng2.normal(size=(10, 10))) mat2[0, :] *= 0.25 mat2[:, 1] *= 0.25 ax = ensure_canvas(initialize=True) max_w2 = max( strwidth_canvas(s, ax=ax) for s in [f"R{i}" for i in range(1, 11)] + [f"C{i}" for i in range(1, 11)] ) chord_diagram(mat2, annotation_track="grid", pre_allocate_tracks={"track_height": max_w2 * 1.3}) def panel_adaptive_labels(x, y): xlim = get_cell_meta_data("xlim") xplot = get_cell_meta_data("xplot") ylim = get_cell_meta_data("ylim") sector_name = get_cell_meta_data("sector.index") if abs(xplot[1] - xplot[0]) < 12: circos.text( float(np.mean(xlim)), ylim[0], sector_name, facing="clockwise", nice_facing=True, adj=(0.0, 0.5), col="red", cex=0.85, ) else: circos.text( float(np.mean(xlim)), ylim[0], sector_name, facing="inside", nice_facing=True, adj=(0.5, 0.0), col="blue", cex=0.85, ) circos.track(track_index=1, panel_fun=panel_adaptive_labels, bg_border=None) circos.clear() Adaptive sector label direction based on sector

title: 15.3 Customize sector axes
text: With a pre-allocated outer track, you can combine standard absolute value axes on the grid track (track_index=2) with custom relative percentage axes in the outer track (track_index=1). Notice that narrow sectors (< 30 degrees) automatically use coarser 50% ticks while wider sectors use 20% ticks: chord_diagram( mat, grid_col=grid_col, annotation_track="grid", pre_allocate_tracks={"track_height": mm_h(5)}, ) for si in get_all_sector_index(): circos.axis(h="top", labels_cex=0.35, sector_index=si, track_index=2) def panel_pct_axes(x, y): xlim = get_cell_meta_data("xlim") ylim = get_cell_meta_data("ylim") sector_name = get_cell_meta_data("sector.index") xplot = get_cell_meta_data("xplot") circos.lines(xlim, [float(np.mean(ylim)), float(np.mean(ylim))], lty=3) by = 0.2 if abs(xplot[1] - xplot[0]) > 30 else 0.5 for p in np.arange(by, 1.0 + 1e-9, by): circos.text( p * (xlim[1] - xlim[0]) + xlim[0], float(np.mean(ylim)) + 0.1, f"{int(round(p * 100))}%", cex=0.4, adj=(0.5, 0.0), nice_facing=True, ) circos.text(float(np.mean(xlim)), 1.0, sector_name, nice_facing=True, adj=(0.5, 0.0)) circos.track(track_index=1, panel_fun=panel_pct_axes, bg_border=None) circos.clear() Dual sector axes combining absolute value ticks and custom percentage labels.

title:
15.4 Put horizontally or
vertically symmetric
text: When row and column sectors form two non-overlapping groups, chord_diagram() automatically centers the two groups around circos.par(start_degree=...). Setting start_degree=0 yields horizontal symmetry across y = 0, while start_degree=90 yields vertical symmetry across x = 0: fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.6, 4.3)) plt.sca(ax1) circos.par(start_degree=0) chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, big_gap=20) ax1.axhline(0, linestyle="--", color="#00000080", linewidth=1.0) circos.clear() plt.sca(ax2) circos.par(start_degree=90) chord_diagram(mat, grid_col=grid_col, big_gap=20) ax2.axvline(0, linestyle="--", color="#00000080", linewidth=1.0) circos.clear() Rotating two-group Chord diagrams for horizontal (start_degree=0) or vertical (start_degree=90) symmetry.

title: 15.5 Compare two Chord diagrams
text: By default, Chord diagram sector widths are normalized to fill 360 - sum(gaps) degrees, so comparing two matrices with different total link weights side-by-side requires putting them on a common scale. circlize-py provides two complementary ways to achieve this: calc_gap() and xmax.

title:
15.5.1 Equal arc scale via
calc_gap()
text: When comparing two non-overlapping two-group matrices where sum(|mat1|) >= sum(|mat2|), calc_gap(mat1, mat2, big_gap=..., small_gap=...) computes the exact big_gap for the second diagram so that one data unit spans the same arc angle in both plots (provided small_gap matches): rng_cmp = np.random.default_rng(77) mat_cmp1 = pd.DataFrame( rng_cmp.integers(1, 21, size=(5, 5)), index=[f"R{i}" for i in range(1, 6)], columns=[f"C{i}" for i in range(1, 6)], ) mat_cmp2 = mat_cmp1 / 2.0 gap = calc_gap(mat_cmp1, mat_cmp2, big_gap=10, small_gap=1) # gap is 79.0 degrees fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.6, 4.5)) plt.sca(ax1) chord_diagram( mat_cmp1, directional=1, grid_col=list(range(1, 6)) * 2, transparency=0.5, big_gap=10, small_gap=1, ) ax1.set_title("mat1 (full scale, big_gap = 10)", fontsize=9.5) circos.clear() plt.sca(ax2) chord_diagram( mat_cmp2, directional=1, grid_col=list(range(1, 6)) * 2, transparency=0.5, big_gap=gap, small_gap=1, ) ax2.set_title(f"mat2 = mat1 / 2 (big_gap = {gap:.1f})", fontsize=9.5) circos.clear() Comparing two Chord diagrams on a common unit scale using calc_gap().

title:
15.5.2 Matching per-sector
capacity via xmax
text: Alternatively, passing xmax (a dict or pd.Series mapping sector names to maximum capacities) fixes the total width of each individual sector across plots, leaving unused empty space on smaller sectors: rs1 = mat_cmp1.abs().sum(axis=1) cs1 = mat_cmp1.abs().sum(axis=0) xmax_map = {**rs1.to_dict(), **cs1.to_dict()} fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.6, 4.5)) plt.sca(ax1) chord_diagram( mat_cmp1, directional=1, grid_col=list(range(1, 6)) * 2, transparency=0.5, big_gap=10, small_gap=1, ) ax1.set_title("mat1 (reference sector widths)", fontsize=9.5) circos.clear() plt.sca(ax2) chord_diagram( mat_cmp2, directional=1, grid_col=list(range(1, 6)) * 2, transparency=0.5, big_gap=10, small_gap=1, xmax=xmax_map, ) ax2.set_title("mat2 with xmax = mat1 sector totals", fontsize=9.5) circos.clear() Comparing two Chord diagrams by pinning per-sector widths with xmax.

title: 15.6 Multiple-group Chord diagram
text: When sectors fall into more than two groups, the group parameter of chord_diagram() automatically orders sectors by group and places big_gap between groups and small_gap within groups. This works identically for matrix and adjacency-list inputs. Let’s construct a 10x10 matrix connecting three groups (A, B, and C): rng = np.random.default_rng(321) mat1 = pd.DataFrame(rng.normal(size=(5, 5)), index=[f"A{i}" for i in range(1, 6)], columns=[f"B{i}" for i in range(1, 6)]) mat2 = pd.DataFrame(rng.normal(size=(5, 5)), index=[f"A{i}" for i in range(1, 6)], columns=[f"C{i}" for i in range(1, 6)]) mat3 = pd.DataFrame(rng.normal(size=(5, 5)), index=[f"B{i}" for i in range(1, 6)], columns=[f"C{i}" for i in range(1, 6)]) mat_g = pd.DataFrame(0.0, index=list(mat2.index) + list(mat3.index), columns=list(mat1.columns) + list(mat2.columns)) mat_g.loc[mat1.index, mat1.columns] = mat1 mat_g.loc[mat2.index, mat2.columns] = mat2 mat_g.loc[mat3.index, mat3.columns] = mat3 nm = list(dict.fromkeys(list(mat_g.index) + list(mat_g.columns))) gcol_g = {s: (2 if s[0] == "A" else (3 if s[0] == "B" else 4)) for s in nm} Pass a dictionary (or pd.Series) mapping each sector name to its group label: group_abc = {s: s[0] for s in nm} chord_diagram(mat_g, group=group_abc, grid_col=gcol_g) circos.clear() Grouped Chord diagram separating sectors into groups A, B, and C. Changing the grouping dictionary immediately regroups the exact same matrix—for example, grouping by trailing index (1 through 5): group_num = {s: s[1:] for s in nm} chord_diagram(mat_g, group=group_num, grid_col=gcol_g) circos.clear() Grouped Chord diagram with sectors grouped by numeric suffix 1–5. In circlize-py, group preserves insertion order of sectors within each group and sorts the group labels lexicographically. Thus, shuffling the key insertion order shuffles within-group sector ordering, and using sortable group labels (such as "1_C", "2_A", "3_B") puts groups in any desired C, A, B sequence: nm_shuffled = list(np.random.default_rng(11).permutation(nm)) prefix_map = {"C": "1_C", "A": "2_A", "B": "3_B"} group_ord = {s: prefix_map[s[0]] for s in nm_shuffled} chord_diagram(mat_g, group=group_ord, grid_col=gcol_g) circos.clear() Controlling group order (C, A, B) and within-group sector permutation via group. Use big_gap and small_gap to tune between-group and within-group spacing: chord_diagram(mat_g, group=group_abc, grid_col=gcol_g, big_gap=20, small_gap=5) circos.clear() Adjusting between-group (big_gap=20) and within-group (small_gap=5) gaps. For a richer multi-group layout, pre-allocate an outer track, place sector labels inside the grid cells (now track 2), and use highlight.sector() on track 1 to draw group-level banners: chord_diagram( mat_g, group=group_abc, grid_col=gcol_g, annotation_track=["grid", "axis"], pre_allocate_tracks={"track_height": mm_h(4), "track_margin": [mm_h(4), 0.0]}, ) circos.track( track_index=2, bg_border=None, panel_fun=lambda x, y: circos.text( CELL_META.xcenter, CELL_META.ycenter, CELL_META.sector_index, cex=0.6, nice_facing=True, ), ) highlight.sector(list(mat1.index), track_index=1, col="red", text="A", cex=0.8, text_col="white", nice_facing=True) highlight.sector(list(mat1.columns), track_index=1, col="green", text="B", cex=0.8, text_col="white", nice_facing=True) highlight.sector(list(mat2.columns), track_index=1, col="blue", text="C", cex=0.8, text_col="white", nice_facing=True) circos.clear() Customized multi-group Chord diagram with group banners drawn via highlight.sector(). Under the hood, group simply computes an ordered sector list and a matching gap_after vector for circos.par(). You can achieve the exact same layout manually with order and circos.par(gap_after=...): ordered_sectors = [s for _, s in sorted((grp, sec) for sec, grp in group_abc.items())] circos.par(gap_after=[1, 1, 1, 1, 5, 1, 1, 1, 1, 5, 1, 1, 1, 1, 5]) chord_diagram(mat_g, order=ordered_sectors, grid_col=gcol_g) circos.clear()

title:
16 A complex example of Chord
diagram
text: In this chapter, we build a publication-grade Chord diagram step by step to visualize chromatin state transitions alongside DNA methylation changes across two sample groups. A chromatin state transition matrix summarizes how many base pairs in the genome switch from one chromatin state in Group 1 to another state in Group 2, while methylation matrices capture the average methylation level of those transitioning regions in each group. The example dataset is processed from the Roadmap Epigenomics 15-state core chromatin model learned from five histone marks (ChromHMM 15-state model). Roadmap samples are split into two expression-based groups, and a chromatin state is assigned to each genomic bin if recurrent in at least half of the group’s samples. Load the pre-converted JSON dataset (data/chromatin_transition.json): import json import matplotlib.patches as mpatches import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd from circlize_py import ( CELL_META, chord_diagram, circos, color_ramp2, color_to_hex, get_cell_meta_data, mm_y, ) with open("data/chromatin_transition.json", encoding="utf-8") as fh: raw = json.load(fh) all_states = list(raw["mat"]["rownames"]) n_states = len(all_states) mat_arr = np.array(raw["mat"]["values"], dtype=float) meth_mat_1 = pd.DataFrame( np.array(raw["meth_mat_1"]["values"], dtype=float), index=all_states, columns=all_states, ) meth_mat_2 = pd.DataFrame( np.array(raw["meth_mat_2"]["values"], dtype=float), index=all_states, columns=all_states, ) The JSON file stores three 15x15 matrices: mat: chromatin state transition matrix where rows represent states in Group 1 and columns represent states in Group 2. Entry (i, j) gives the total base pairs transitioning from state i in Group 1 to state j in Group 2 (for example, TssA to TxFlnk). Diagonal entries correspond to regions whose state remains unchanged between groups. meth_mat_1: mean DNA methylation in Group 1 for regions transitioning from row state i to column state j (null in JSON maps to NaN when zero base pairs are observed). meth_mat_2: mean DNA methylation in Group 2 for the same transitioning regions. pd.DataFrame(mat_arr[:4, :4], index=all_states[:4], columns=all_states[:4]) TssA TssAFlnk TxFlnk Tx TssA 497200.0 79600.0 13400.0 1800.0 TssAFlnk 56400.0 233200.0 5000.0 800.0 TxFlnk 0.0 400.0 43000.0 1800.0 Tx 800.0 200.0 200.0 166400.0 Across the genome, most regions (~61.9%) keep the same chromatin state in both groups. To focus exclusively on state switches, we record that proportion and zero out the diagonal: unchanged_prop = float(np.trace(mat_arr) / np.sum(mat_arr)) # ~0.619226 np.fill_diagonal(mat_arr, 0.0) Because Group 1 and Group 2 represent distinct sample groups even though they share the 15 state names, we assign distinct row and column identifiers (R_1..R_15 and C_1..C_15) while preserving the original names in all_states: rn = [f"R_{i}" for i in range(1, n_states + 1)] cn = [f"C_{i}" for i in range(1, n_states + 1)] mat = pd.DataFrame(mat_arr, index=rn, columns=cn) meth_mat_1.index, meth_mat_1.columns = rn, cn meth_mat_2.index, meth_mat_2.columns = rn, cn Next, we assign group colors (red for active states 1–8, blue for repressed/bivalent states 9–14, and black for quiescent state 15) and build a 2D link-color array colmat. Major transitions above the 70th percentile receive higher opacity ("A0") while minor transitions fade into the background ("20"): state_col = { "TssA": "#E41A1C", "TssAFlnk": "#E41A1C", "TxFlnk": "#E41A1C", "Tx": "#E41A1C", "TxWk": "#E41A1C", "EnhG": "#E41A1C", "Enh": "#E41A1C", "ZNF/Rpts": "#E41A1C", "Het": "#377EB8", "TssBiv": "#377EB8", "BivFlnk": "#377EB8", "EnhBiv": "#377EB8", "ReprPC": "#377EB8", "ReprPCWk": "#377EB8", "Quies": "black", } state_col2 = {} for i, st in enumerate(all_states, start=1): state_col2[f"R_{i}"] = state_col[st] state_col2[f"C_{i}"] = state_col[st] qati = float(np.quantile(mat_arr, 0.7)) colmat = np.empty(mat_arr.shape, dtype=object) for i in range(n_states): hx = c

title: 17 Make fun of the package
text: Because circlize-py provides low-level circular geometry primitives (circos.axis(), circos.text(), circos.rect(), draw.sector()) on top of Matplotlib, it can also draw playful non-genomic circular graphics. Below are three classic examples.

title: 17.1 A clock
text: The first example draws an analog clock face. The key function is circos.axis() inside a single full-circle sector where major tick 0 overlaps with major tick 12. After setting up the dial (0–12 ticks and downward hour labels), we compute the angles of the second, minute, and hour hands from the current wall-clock time (datetime.now()) and draw the hands directly in canvas coordinates ([-1, 1] x [-1, 1]) with Matplotlib’s ax.annotate(): from datetime import datetime import math import numpy as np from circlize_py import circos, ensure_canvas, mm_y ax = ensure_canvas(initialize=True) circos.par(gap_degree=0, cell_padding=(0, 0, 0, 0), start_degree=90) circos.initialize("a", xlim=(0, 12)) circos.track(ylim=(0, 1), bg_border=None) circos.axis( major_at=np.arange(0, 13), labels=None, direction="inside", major_tick_length=mm_y(2), ) circos.text( np.arange(1, 13), np.repeat(1.0, 12) - mm_y(6), [str(h) for h in range(1, 13)], facing="downward", ) now = datetime.now() sec = now.second + (1 if now.microsecond > 0 else 0) minute = now.minute hour = now.hour % 12 sec_rad = math.radians(90.0 - sec / 60.0 * 360.0) min_rad = math.radians(90.0 - minute / 60.0 * 360.0) hour_rad = math.radians(90.0 - hour / 12.0 * 360.0 - minute / 60.0 * 360.0 / 12.0) ax.annotate( "", xy=(math.cos(sec_rad) * 0.8, math.sin(sec_rad) * 0.8), xytext=(0.0, 0.0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="black", lw=1.0, mutation_scale=12), ) ax.annotate( "", xy=(math.cos(min_rad) * 0.7, math.sin(min_rad) * 0.7), xytext=(0.0, 0.0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="black", lw=2.0, mutation_scale=14), ) ax.annotate( "", xy=(math.cos(hour_rad) * 0.4, math.sin(hour_rad) * 0.4), xytext=(0.0, 0.0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="black", lw=2.2, mutation_scale=14), ) circos.clear() A clock.

title: 17.2 A dartboard
text: The second example builds a regulation 20-sector dartboard. Five tracks with custom track_height values form the number ring, double ring, outer single area, triple ring, and inner single area, while two draw.sector() calls add the outer green bullseye (rou1=0.1) and inner red bullseye (rou1=0.05). Setting start_degree=360/20/2 (9 degrees) and clock_wise=False aligns sector 20 vertically at 12 o’clock, and circos.track_text() places the sector scores around the black outer ring: import numpy as np from circlize_py import circos, draw sectors = [str(i) for i in range(1, 21)] dart_labels = [13, 4, 18, 1, 20, 5, 12, 9, 14, 11, 8, 16, 7, 19, 3, 17, 2, 15, 10, 6] circos.par( gap_degree=0, cell_padding=(0, 0, 0, 0), start_degree=360.0 / 20.0 / 2.0, track_margin=(0, 0), clock_wise=False, ) circos.initialize(sectors, xlim=(0, 1)) circos.track(ylim=(0, 1), sectors=sectors, bg_col="black", track_height=0.15) circos.track_text( x=np.repeat(0.5, 20), y=np.repeat(0.5, 20), labels=[str(v) for v in dart_labels], cex=0.85, sectors=sectors, col="#EEEEEE", font=2, facing="downward", ) circos.track( ylim=(0, 1), sectors=sectors, bg_col=["#E41A1C", "#4DAF4A"] * 10, bg_border="#EEEEEE", track_height=0.05, ) circos.track( ylim=(0, 1), sectors=sectors, bg_col=["black", "white"] * 10, bg_border="#EEEEEE", track_height=0.275, ) circos.track( ylim=(0, 1), sectors=sectors, bg_col=["#E41A1C", "#4DAF4A"] * 10, bg_border="#EEEEEE", track_height=0.05, ) circos.track( ylim=(0, 1), sectors=sectors, bg_col=["black", "white"] * 10, bg_border="#EEEEEE", track_height=0.375, ) draw.sector(center=(0, 0), start_degree=0, end_degree=360, rou1=0.1, col="#4DAF4A", border="#EEEEEE") draw.sector(center=(0, 0), start_degree=0, end_degree=360, rou1=0.05, col="#E41A1C", border="#EEEEEE") circos.clear() A dartboard.

title: 17.3 Ba-Gua and Tai-Ji
text: The third example renders Ba-Gua and the central Tai-Ji symbol using circos.rect() and draw.sector(). Ba-Gua originated in ancient Chinese philosophy thousands of years ago, combining two basic signs—the solid Yang line (add_yang_yao) and the broken Yin line (add_yin_yao)—across three concentric tracks and eight sectors to form the eight trigrams. At the center sits Tai-Ji, representing duality and continuous mutual transformation between complementary opposites (Yin and Yang), each containing a seed of the other: from circlize_py import CELL_META, circos, draw, get_cell_meta_data sectors = [str(i) for i in range(1, 9)] circos.par(start_degree=22.5, gap_degree=6) circos.initialize(sectors, xlim=(0, 1)) # Yang yao is a single solid bar def add_yang_yao(): circos.rect(0, 0, 1, 1, col="black") # Yin yao is a broken bar (two segments) def add_yin_yao(): circos.rect(0, 0, 0.45, 1, col="black") circos.rect(0.55, 0, 1, 1, col="black") circos.track( ylim=(0, 1), sectors=sectors, bg_border=None, track_height=0.1, panel_fun=lambda x, y: add_yang_yao() if CELL_META.sector_numeric_index in {2, 5, 7, 8} else add_yin_yao(), ) circos.track( ylim=(0, 1), sectors=sectors, bg_border=None, track_height=0.1, panel_fun=lambda x, y: add_yang_yao() if CELL_META.sector_numeric_index in {1, 6, 7, 8} else add_yin_yao(), ) circos.track( ylim=(0, 1), sectors=sectors, bg_border=None, track_height=0.1, panel_fun=lambda x, y: add_yang_yao() if CELL_META.sector_numeric_index in {4, 5, 6, 7} else add_yin_yao(), ) # Bottom radius of the innermost track r = float(get_cell_meta_data("cell.bottom.radius")) - 0.1 # Draw Tai-Ji (default draw.sector direction is clockwise) draw.sector(center=(0, 0), start_degree=90, end_degree=-90, rou1=r, col="black", border="black") draw.sector(center=(0, 0), start_degree=270, end_degree=90, rou1=r, col="white", border="black") draw.sector(center=(0, r / 2), start_degree=0, end_degree=360, rou1=r / 2, col="white", border="white") draw.sector(center=(0, -r / 2), start_degree=0, end_degree=360, rou1=r / 2, col="black", border="black") draw.sector(center=(0, r / 2), start_degree=0, end_degree=360, rou1=r / 8, col="black", border="black") draw.sector(center=(0, -r / 2), start_degree=0, end_degree=360, rou1=r / 8, col="white", border="white") circos.clear() Ba-Gua and Tai-Ji.
